title: Safe Reinforcement Learning from Operator Feedback for Fusion Control: Imitation and Policy Exploration Confined to a Control-Barrier-Certified Safe Set
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves a controller by exploring, and on a nuclear fusion plant unconstrained exploration is precisely what must never happen. We formalise and demonstrate safe reinforcement learning from operator feedback for the Kronos controller of a compact negative-triangularity spherical-tokamak breeder (design point operating limit 3.5; I_p=9.66 MA, Q=3.076, P_fus=85.04 MW, δ=-0.30, B_0=8 T, κ=2.0, R_0=1.20 m, aspect ratio A=2.5). The design separates the two questions that safe learning usually conflates. Where may the policy act? is answered once, by a control-barrier-function (CBF) certified safe set C=\x:(x) 3.5\ that no exploratory action may leave; how may it improve inside that set? is answered by learning from the operators themselves. We state the reduced plant, the safe set, the discrete-time CBF forward-invariance condition, the minimal-intervention quadratic-program (QP) safety filter, and the operator-feedback objective (behavioural cloning plus a twin-scored override reward) as explicit equations, and we cast policy admission as pre-registered inequalities. The safety guarantee is demonstrated, not asserted: over a 100-step closed-loop exploration campaign the shielded policy records zero limit crossings against 50 for the unshielded policy, holding the peak at the boundary (=3.500 versus 4.200) with the barrier value non-negative throughout (_k h=+0.000, forward invariance) and a bounded actuation u[1.061,1.250] that never reaches the available floor u_=0.5, so the certificate is not authority-limited. The learning update is disciplined by an active-learning designer whose information gain beats random selection (grounded in a 200-evaluation surrogate Bayesian-optimisation campaign that returns a calibrated confinement posterior H_98=1.007±0.030 bounding how far the policy may explore), a continual-learning scheme that shows no regression on the validated benchmark, and a gated promotion step that admits only models passing a 19/19 verification suite with automatic rollback. Beyond per-step feasibility we state a closed-loop input-to-state-stability (ISS) certificate — a learned Lyapunov function co-verified with the policy — so that the plant not only never leaves C but provably returns toward its setpoint after a disturbance; and we place the whole learned loop inside a Simplex runtime-assurance architecture in which a formally verified baseline controller reclaims authority near the boundary and an actuator-independent hardware trip forms an unconditional last line of defense, so that safety is enforced structurally, in three certified floors, and never delegated to the learner. Every quantitative claim traces to a frozen, independently reproduced anchor in the Kronos de-risking register. The result is a controller that gets better from the people who run it without ever leaving the set that is proven safe. Key results (frozen anchors): H_98 = 1.007 ±0.030; sigma = 5 %. Methods & codes: FreeGSNKE, FreeGS, CGYRO, Sauter. Live verification: 3 gate validator(s) with live-recompute cards (3 reproduced). See the Verification section and data/verification.csv. Related: Paper page · De-risking register · 3D model · Learn more about Kronos Part of the 2026 Kronos publication series; independently re-run and stamped in the Kronos de-risking register (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22645689). All numerical values are frozen design-point anchors; see the register. Public research artifact. No proprietary, financial, or supply-chain information is included.

title: Dataset for: Evaluating multimodal large language model (LLM) systems on a Transport Canada Private Pilot Licence (PPL) Exam
abstract: This dataset accompanies a study evaluating the performance of contemporary consumer-facing multimodal large language model (LLM) systems on an official Transport Canada Private Pilot Licence (PPL) sample written examination (TP 13014). Fifteen AI system configurations from OpenAI/ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and Microsoft Copilot were evaluated. Each configuration completed the same examination on three independent occasions using a standardised zero-shot prompt and a fresh chat session for each run. The models were supplied with the examination in PDF format and were required to return answers to all 100 multiple-choice questions without iterative prompting or access to the official answer key. The workbook contains the complete model responses for all three runs, the official answer key used for scoring, per-question correct/incorrect classifications, and adjusted sectional performance data. Transport Canada divides the examination into Air Law, Aeronautics, Meteorology, and Navigation sections and requires both an overall passing score and minimum performance within each section. Eleven Navigation questions depended on a Toronto VFR Navigation Chart that was referenced by the examination but was not available with the publicly accessible source material. These questions were retained in the raw response data but excluded from the primary adjusted analysis. Adjusted overall performance is therefore calculated from 89 valid questions, with the Navigation section calculated from the nine questions that could be answered using the material supplied to the models.

title: Hippocampus-Inspired Artificial Neural Network Enables Robust Classification under Sparsity: Structured versus Brute-Force Robustness
abstract: Introduction We investigate robustness to structural sparsity in a hippocampus-inspired artificial neural network (OurANN) for image classification. OurANN is composed of functional modules—dentate gyrus (DG), CA3, and CA1—rather than conventional hidden layers (see Figure 1). DG enforces sparse competitive representations, CA3 provides recurrent stabilization, CA1 integrates stabilized activity for readout, and shortcut connections (EC→CA3 and EC→CA1) preserve signal flow under sparse connectivity. Methods As a baseline, we use a conventional multilayer perceptron (CANN) with three feedforward hidden layers whose numbers of units match those of DG, CA3, and CA1. Our ANN classifier is trained using standard backpropagation (Ref. [1]), ensuring direct comparability with the CANN baseline. Using the MNIST dataset as a controlled benchmark, we sweep the inter-layer connection probability pc from 1.0 down to 0.01 and evaluate robustness using global degradation rates and robustness indices, together with local performance metrics. Results In the dense and moderate regimes (pc=1.0 ~ 0.1), OurANN and CANN exhibit nearly identical performance, indicating no intrinsic advantage under weak sparsity. Differences begin to emerge in the sparse regime (pc = 0.1 ~ 0.05), where OurANN shows slower performance degradation, in contrast to the CANN. In the extremely sparse regime (pc = 0.05 ~ 0.01), OurANN exhibits clear and persistent robustness, while CANN performance rapidly collapses. Discussion Although CANN robustness can be partially recovered through brute-force scaling of layer size, achieving robustness comparable to OurANN requires substantially increased parameter redundancy. These results distinguish structural robustness in OurANN, arising from hippocampus-inspired architectural organization, from brute-force scaling robustness in CANN, achieved through parameter expansion. Figure Figure 1: Hippocampus-inspired artificial neural network (ANN). Feedforward: EC (entorhinal cortex) → DG (dentate gyrus) → CA3 and Shortcuts (SCs): EC → CA3 and EC → CA1 and inhibitory backprojection: CA3 → DG. S: subiculum. References [1] Rumelhart, D. E., Hinton, G. E., & Williams, R. J (1986) Learning representations by back-propagating errors Nature, 323, 533-536

title: 基于自适应的神经元网络架构
abstract: The design of novel neural network architectures is an ongoing area of research with significant implications for machine learning across diverse domains. This paper introduces a novel architecture, termed "Adaptive Neural Network" (ANN), which dynamically adjusts the connection weights and activation functions of neurons based on the characteristics of incoming data. This adaptive mechanism aims to improve model performance, particularly in situations involving complex data distributions. The core of this architecture is a self-tuning neural network structure, leveraging a learning and adjustment process to optimize network behavior. This approach offers a potential advantage over traditional architectures in terms of robustness and generalization, addressing a key challenge in machine learning. The paper details the design, implementation, and evaluation of the ANN, demonstrating its effectiveness through illustrative examples and quantitative analysis.

title: Quantum Entanglement Amplification and Adaptive Quantum Computing
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, has long been a subject of intense theoretical and experimental investigation. While the phenomenon of entanglement is well-established, its potential for practical applications, particularly in computation, remains largely unexplored. This paper explores the extension of quantum entanglement to facilitate adaptive quantum computation, utilizing a novel non-local model and an optimized quantum algorithm. We argue that the introduction of non-local effects, coupled with adaptive algorithms, offers a pathway towards solving complex problems intractable with classical approaches. The core claim is that by leveraging this framework, we can achieve significant advancements in quantum computation, particularly through enhanced complexity handling.

title: Probabilistic Programming for Counterfactual Inference with Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Counterfactual reasoning – the ability to reason about what *would* have happened if something had been different – is crucial for understanding complex systems, particularly multi-agent systems. However, applying counterfactual methods in this domain is significantly challenging due to the intricate interplay between agents and their environment. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging probabilistic programming to address this challenge. We propose a framework that explicitly models agent dynamics, communication, and environmental constraints within a probabilistic setting, allowing for the systematic exploration of counterfactual scenarios. The core of our approach lies in the development of a probabilistic programming language designed to facilitate the definition and execution of these scenarios. We demonstrate the utility of this framework through a theoretical analysis, highlighting its potential for uncovering causal relationships and predicting outcomes under alternative conditions. The key contributions are a formal representation of counterfactual reasoning in multi-agent systems and a practical tool for its implementation.

title: Quantum-Inspired Data Stream Anomaly Detection
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-inspired principles to enhance anomaly detection within data streams. Traditional anomaly detection methods often rely on statistical models and thresholding, which can be inefficient and inaccurate when dealing with rapidly changing data streams. We propose a novel approach that leverages concepts analogous to superposition and interference, treating data stream segments as quantum states. This allows for the simultaneous exploration of multiple potential patterns and the identification of anomalies through interference effects, where deviations from expected patterns lead to a reduction in the overall probability amplitude. The core of our methodology involves constructing a quantum-inspired state representation of the stream and employing techniques resembling quantum measurement to identify deviations. We demonstrate the theoretical foundations of this approach and outline a framework for its implementation, highlighting its potential advantages over conventional methods in terms of sensitivity and efficiency. The key contribution lies in providing a tangible and computationally feasible method for integrating quantum-inspired ideas into a real-time data analysis scenario, specifically anomaly detection.

title: Formal Verification of Probabilistic Programming Languages using Markov Logic Networks
abstract: Probabilistic programming languages (PPLs) offer a powerful approach to modeling uncertainty and reasoning under incomplete information. However, ensuring the correctness of these programs – particularly when dealing with complex probabilistic models – remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes a novel framework for formally verifying the behavior of PPLs by leveraging Markov Logic Networks (MLNs). MLNs provide a mathematical representation of logical constraints, enabling a systematic approach to verifying program behavior under specified assumptions. The core idea is to translate a probabilistic program into an MLN representation, then utilize the MLN's inference capabilities to check if the program satisfies a given set of logical rules. We demonstrate that this approach offers a viable path toward addressing the computational intractability inherent in traditional verification techniques for probabilistic programs. The paper outlines the methodology, key concepts, and potential limitations of this approach.

title: Adaptive Nonlinear Model Parameter Optimization Framework
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive nonlinear model parameter optimization framework designed to address the challenges of optimizing complex non-linear models, particularly within the realms of machine learning and deep learning. Traditional parameter optimization methods often employ static parameter settings, hindering the ability to effectively improve model generalization and performance. Our proposed framework dynamically adjusts model parameters based on training error and gradient information, leading to a more robust and efficient optimization process. The core mechanism leverages an adaptive algorithm to continuously refine model parameters, offering a significant improvement over static optimization techniques. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework through comprehensive analysis and illustrative examples across various machine learning tasks.

title: Quantum Simulator Based on Geometric Modeling
abstract: Quantum simulation, a crucial tool for understanding complex quantum systems, has long been hampered by computational limitations. Traditional methods often struggle to accurately represent the intricate quantum behavior of large systems. This paper introduces a novel quantum simulator, Quantum Simulator Based on Geometric Modeling, which leverages the power of geometric modeling to enhance the fidelity of quantum simulations. We propose a framework where the quantum system's geometry is explicitly defined and utilized to guide the simulation process, leading to improved accuracy and efficiency, particularly for systems with intricate spatial dependencies. The core mechanism centers around meticulously constructing geometric representations of quantum systems, enabling a more precise mapping of quantum states and interactions. This approach addresses limitations of existing methods by offering a fundamentally new way to control and interpret quantum phenomena.

title: 基于多智能体协同的复杂系统建模 (Multi-Agent Collaborative Modeling of Complex Systems - MACCS)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to complex systems modeling, termed Multi-Agent Collaborative Modeling of Complex Systems (MACCS). The core claim is that effective modeling of complex systems necessitates a collaborative framework utilizing multiple intelligent agents. The proposed mechanism involves constructing a system comprised of numerous agents, each responsible for simulating a specific aspect of the complex system. These agents then interact through information sharing and decision-making processes. This approach offers a fundamentally new perspective on complex system modeling, shifting away from monolithic representations towards a distributed, agent-based methodology. The paper details the theoretical framework, outlines a potential implementation strategy, and discusses key considerations for successful MACCS deployment. Ultimately, MACCS aims to improve the accuracy, scalability, and interpretability of complex systems models.

title: Differentiable Quantum Circuit Design Language
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Differentiable Quantum Circuit Design Language (DQCDL), designed to facilitate automated quantum algorithm design through direct optimization within the circuit's parameter space. The core concept revolves around representing quantum circuits as sets of differentiable parameters and constructing a gradient model for these circuits. Utilizing optimization algorithms like gradient descent, the DQCDL enables the iterative adjustment of circuit parameters, leading to the efficient optimization of quantum algorithms. This approach contrasts with traditional manual parameter tuning methods, offering a significantly more streamlined and automated process for quantum circuit design and optimization. The paper details the language's syntax, the methodology for building the gradient model, and outlines the optimization strategies applicable within the DQCDL framework. The primary goal is to provide a framework for exploring the vast design space of quantum circuits, ultimately accelerating the development and deployment of quantum algorithms.

title: Dynamically Reconfigurable Neural Networks with Hardware-Level Control
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network design—Dynamically Reconfigurable Neural Networks (DRNNs)—that addresses the limitations of static neural networks by incorporating hardware-level control. The core idea is to create a neural network architecture where connections between nodes can be reconfigured in real-time, adapting to fluctuating computational demands. This is achieved through a dedicated hardware system that monitors network activity and physically adjusts the connections based on learned patterns and predefined rules. The architecture utilizes a layered approach with a central control unit that manages the reconfiguration process, alongside processing nodes that execute the neural network computations. The theoretical framework outlines the key components and the mathematical models used to describe the network's behavior and the reconfiguration process. The system is designed to improve computational efficiency and responsiveness, particularly in dynamic environments. The presented approach offers a fundamentally new way to build neural networks, merging the flexibility of learning with the performance advantages of hardware-level control.

title: 基于多模态隐式语义向量的知识图谱推理
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge graph (KG) reasoning leveraging multi-modal implicit semantic vector representations. Traditional KG reasoning methods often rely heavily on symbolic logic, which can be computationally expensive and struggle with the complexities inherent in real-world knowledge. Our approach addresses this limitation by embedding data from various modalities – text, images, and audio – into a unified vector space. We construct a multi-modal embedding model to map these different modalities into a shared space, allowing for reasoning based on semantic similarity rather than explicit rules. The core claim of this work is that this multi-modal representation significantly improves the accuracy of KG reasoning. The key mechanism involves utilizing vector similarity measures to infer relationships between entities within the KG. This method avoids the limitations of traditional symbolic approaches by harnessing the pattern recognition capabilities of deep learning. Experimental results, although not presented in this document due to the focus on the methodology, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

title: Quantumization of Consensus Mechanisms
abstract: This paper explores the novel concept of quantumizing classical consensus mechanisms, specifically drawing inspiration from algorithms like Paxos. The core idea revolves around encoding the state of a consensus process – such as agreement on a value – into quantum bits (qubits) and leveraging quantum entanglement for accelerated communication and voting. Traditional consensus algorithms often suffer from performance bottlenecks due to the limitations of classical communication and the inherent latency of distributed systems. By employing quantum mechanics, particularly entanglement, we propose a pathway to significantly enhance the efficiency and speed of achieving consensus. This work outlines the theoretical framework for this approach, detailing the mapping of classical states to quantum states, the utilization of entanglement for rapid information exchange, and a preliminary analysis of the potential advantages. While this research does not involve experimental validation, it lays a foundational understanding for future exploration in this burgeoning field. The primary contribution is a conceptual model that demonstrates the feasibility of translating classical consensus protocols into a quantum paradigm.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of formalizing logic as a system of modular, interconnected sub-systems, emphasizing the emergence of behavior through interactions and constraints. Traditional approaches often struggle to adequately model emergent properties, necessitating a paradigm shift towards a system that intrinsically anticipates and responds to complex interactions. The core claim is that formalizing logic inherently supports this emergent behavior, offering a robust framework for analyzing and understanding complex systems across various domains. This work investigates the potential of this approach, demonstrating its theoretical foundations and preliminary experimental validation of its capabilities.

title: Behind the screen: laypersons' mental models about ChatGPT
abstract: Introduction ChatGPT's conversational interface invites anthropomorphic interpretations that conflict with its underlying probabilistic architecture. Prior research has identified folk theories and conceptions of generative AI among technical laypersons, but has largely examined these mental concepts in isolation or at the group level. Less is known about how conceptualizations of ChatGPT as a deterministic, probabilistic, anthropomorphic or dynamic AI system coexist, interact, and contradict one another within technical laypersons. This study examined (RQ1) recurring qualitative mental model configurations of ChatGPT among participants and (RQ2) whether technical AI terminology was supported by mechanism-specific understanding or coexisted with misconceptions concerning the same or another functional mechanism. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with technical laypersons ( N = 21) to ask them about their understanding of how ChatGPT works. Statements were deductively coded into four mental concepts (deterministic, probabilistic, anthropomorphic, and dynamic). Mental models were constructed for each participant. Statements containing technical terminology were additionally classified according to whether the term was contradicted by the participant's explanation of the same mechanism (“Chauffeur Knowledge”) or co-occurred with a misconception in another mechanism. Results Three recurring mental model configurations emerged: (i) Predominantly Probabilistic Thinking Patterns ( n = 8); (ii) Anthropomorphic and Dynamic Thinking Patterns ( n = 4), characterized by limited probabilistic reasoning; and (iii) Predominantly Deterministic Retrieval-based Thinking Patterns ( n = 9), characterized mainly by deterministic conceptions alongside limited probabilistic awareness. All participants showed at least one misconception about ChatGPT and among 10 participants, who used technical terminology in their explanations, seven showed chauffeur knowledge, seven demonstrated correct or partially correct understanding of one mechanism alongside a misconception about another, and four participants met both criteria. Discussion Participants' mental models of ChatGPT are fragmented and often internally contradictory. Technical terminology may mask misunderstanding of the mechanism it describes or coexist with correct understanding in one domain and misconceptions in another. These findings challenge AI literacy assessments that rely predominantly on knowledge of technical terminology. Identifying recurring qualitative configurations provides a basis for developing measures that capture the complexity of mental models and may improve predictions of over-reliance on ChatGPT output.

title: Quantum Wavefunction Augmentation via Variational Autoencoders
abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) has emerged as a promising route for quantum-centric supercomputing, relying on classical diagonalization of the molecular Hamiltonian within a hardware-sampled determinant subspace. However, its accuracy degrades in strongly correlated regimes where the relevant determinant space exceeds what finite-shot sampling can capture. In this work, we introduce Quantum Wavefunction Augmentation via Variational Autoencoders (Q-WAVE), a hybrid method that combines determinants sampled via SqDRIFT Krylov circuits and configuration interaction singles and doubles (CISD) determinants with generative machine learning. Using a custom $β$-annealed variational autoencoder (VAE) model, Q-WAVE iteratively expands this basis toward the variational ground state. The VAE learns the wavefunction's primary support structure from the combined hardware and CISD seed in a continuous latent space, generating new dominant determinants beyond any fixed excitation hierarchy. The resulting compact wavefunction exceeds what can be extracted from raw hardware samples alone. We demonstrate sub-millihartree accuracy compared to full configuration interaction for $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{N}_2$ dissociation. Finally, we establish Q-WAVE's scalability on a 52-qubit ethylene system (achieving sub-millihartree accuracy versus CCSD(T)) and a highly correlated 60-qubit $\text{Cr}_2$ stress test that attains chemical accuracy upon a final perturbative correction.

title: Nothing Breaks: No Single Peer Can Soundly Gate Post-Quantum Delivery
abstract: Post-quantum protection is delivered to a peer, not declared in a file: whether a session is quantum-resistant is a relation between a server's configuration and the clients that reach it. We show that no single peer can soundly gate that relation. Shipped SSH clients are not ordered: two of their post-quantum capability classes are minimal and incomparable, so a check pinned to either misses the other family's withdrawal. A peer taking both fares no better: it falls back and misses both, or, where classical outranks one family, catches just that one. No case flags both. Nothing above the wire carries the relation either. An artifact-side instrument cannot encode it, because a peer population is not one of its inputs; and across seven configurations on two protocols we find that not one of the five scalars deployed auditors expose to automation moves, while unrelated degradation moves the ones that discriminate at all: the auditors do compute the delivered algorithm, and discard it at the interface automation reads. Nothing else catches the loss either, because nothing breaks: removing a hybrid key exchange starts the daemon, validates the configuration, passes the tests and serves the client, and the adversary it defends against does not exist yet, so no functional signal can carry the loss even in principle. We then show that agents make that state reachable at scale, driving a validated downgrade in 40 of 40 episodes from ordinary engineering prose, against 0 of 40 on a matched neutral document.

title: ADAPTIVE CONTEXT MANAGEMENT IN LONG-CONTEXT GENERATIVE AI SYSTEMS - A VALIDATION-ORIENTED FRAMEWORK
abstract: Long-context generative artificial intelligence systems are no longer isolated neural models. When used, the UIs, retrievers, vector store, memory service, tool controller, safety filter, model runtime, cache, and accelerator infrastructure together provide a response to the user. This paper depicts how adaptive context management may be formulated as a cross-layer systems problem arising from long-context large language models and retrieval-augmented generation. The paper consolidates work on Transformers, long-context evaluation, RAG, GraphRAG, KGG-RAG, agentic RAG, memory systems, MCP-style tool connectivity, guardrails, verification, efficient inference, and telecom-focused deployment. The key contribution is a five-layer Adaptive Context Management Framework comprising the application, processing, model, data-memory and infrastructure layers. According to this framework, context is a rare resource that decays over time. Context selection approaches are formulated as an optimization problem, constrained utility optimization, to optimize relevance and source authority, freshness, memory importance, token/compute cost, privacy/security risk. The paper also outlines quantifiable validation metrics such as evidence support ratio, risk of hallucination score, latency decomposition, energy proxy, and multi-objective context-policy utility. The recommended system is described as additive to Sself-RAG, GraphRAG, Agentic RAG, MCP-like device accessibility, and long context model interfaces, not alternative to those. Since no claim is made of implementation results, I will frame the contribution as a framework/blueprint of validation-oriented research. A telecom focused validation plan will be proposed using anonymized or synthetic network logs, configuration changes, vendor manuals, incident tickets, alarms, policy documents etc. The argument presented in the paper is that larger context windows and fixed top-k retrieval alone cannot solve the issues of context dilution, lost-in-the-middle, stale memory, retrieval noise, prompt injection, privacy leakage, latency growth, and energy cost.

title: GeoProofBench v0.1: a machine-checked proposition set for digital elevation model analysis
abstract: Digital elevation model (DEM) analysis underlies terrain-related work across geomorphology, hydrology, and civil engineering, yet published algorithms are rarely machine-checked. GeoProofBench (GPB) v0.1 is a proposition set of terrain-analysis claims expressed in Dafny and Lean 4, with a reproducible pipeline that compiles each proposition to a numerical witness, a Wolfram symbolic check, and a manim visualization, keyed to a GPB-N ENTRY: PASS verdict. This deposit contains six first-order operators, composition records (including fill-then-watershed), counter-example grids, five noise levels, four DEM stacks plus three public product windows (USGS 3DEP lidar, Alaska IFSAR, Copernicus GLO-30), Dafny/Lean sources, Python/Wolfram drivers, and mp4 animations. Data are licensed CC-BY-4.0; software is licensed MIT. Public file access is intended at journal acceptance; until then the record may be restricted.

title: CCC Structural Folding Runtime: Metric Clustering, Structural Merge, and Runtime Localization
abstract: CCC Structural Folding Runtime (CSFR) is a general structural runtime framework for transforming metric-space object collections into folded CCC structures that support runtime dispatch, structural localization, and localized intelligence. CSFR distinguishes object-to-object distance (D_PP), object-to-CCC distance (D_PC), and CCC-to-CCC distance (D_CC); introduces policy-compressed Cluster CCCs and aligned Sequence Claw-Dragon Merge; and extends runtime search through CCC DNA, reverse structural indexing, Two-Way CCC, and Two-Phase Structural Search. The canonical runtime progression is: Metric -> Cluster -> Merge -> CCC -> DNA -> Retrieve -> Verify -> Localization. The repository also includes Stock-Market Structural Folding as the first canonical application case, demonstrating how historical metric-space patterns can be folded into runtime-localizable structural regimes while keeping structural localization distinct from downstream prediction.

title: High-Dimensional Space Distribution Probability Modeling Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of machine learning to optimize probability models for high-dimensional space distributions. Traditional approaches often rely on manual parameter tuning, presenting challenges in terms of computational cost and model robustness. We propose a novel model that leverages machine learning to automatically adjust model parameters, resulting in improved predictive accuracy. The core mechanism centers around establishing a probabilistic model for high-dimensional space distributions, utilizing machine learning to iteratively refine the model's parameters to enhance accuracy. This research addresses a key need in probabilistic modeling, offering a more efficient and adaptable approach compared to traditional methods. The paper presents a detailed analysis of the model's performance, highlighting the benefits of automated parameter optimization.

title: Non-Euclidean Geometry and Quantum Entanglement Models
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-Euclidean geometry to quantum entanglement, proposing a novel model that leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to create novel computational paradigms. The core mechanism centers on the design of a non-Euclidean geometric framework rooted in quantum entanglement, investigating its potential within quantum information processing and quantum algorithm development. We aim to demonstrate how this model can provide a new perspective on geometric principles and potentially unlock advanced computational capabilities. This work investigates the implications of exploring the interplay between geometric intuition and quantum entanglement.

title: Title: Self-Organizing Constraint Networks for Adaptive Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the application of self-organizing constraint networks (SOCN) to adaptive evolutionary algorithms, aiming to improve the robustness and efficiency of optimization processes. SOCN leverages the inherent adaptability of constraint networks, combined with feedback loops, to dynamically adjust constraint parameters during the evolution of a solution. The core mechanism centers around nodes that iteratively adjust their constraints based on the algorithm's performance, fostering a self-optimizing structure that mitigates local optima and explores the solution space more effectively. We propose a framework that allows the network to learn and adapt its constraints, leading to improved convergence and solution quality. This work contributes to the development of more effective evolutionary algorithms capable of handling complex, dynamic problem spaces.

title: Title: Adaptive Probability Space Construction
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Probability Space Construction, a novel method for building probabilistic space. The core principle centers around iteratively constructing a 'probability landscape' through reinforcement learning, meticulously balancing the model's inherent randomness with predictive power. The method leverages a 'Probabilistic Landscape Generator' that utilizes reinforcement learning to construct a network of probabilities, ensuring a dynamic and adaptable system. This approach aims to address limitations in traditional probabilistic modeling by providing a framework for inherent randomness and predictive performance. The concept is predicated on the idea of learning a 'landscape' of probabilities, where each point represents a possible outcome and the system learns to navigate and exploit these landscapes to maximize predictive accuracy. We present a theoretical framework outlining the key components and potential challenges of this method, demonstrating its adaptability through illustrative examples.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Compression (QEDC)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to distributed compression, termed Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Compression (QEDC), leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to surpass the theoretical limits of conventional compression algorithms. The core concept involves establishing entangled states between multiple nodes and exploiting their correlated measurements for data redundancy reduction. We detail the theoretical framework, focusing on the efficiency gains achieved through entanglement-based encoding and correction. Unlike traditional distributed compression methods reliant on classical communication, QEDC offers the potential for significantly higher compression ratios and enhanced security. The presented model employs quantum key distribution protocols to maximize data transmission efficiency. Mathematical formulations are provided to illustrate the key processes involved, including entanglement generation, measurement protocols, and error correction strategies. The architecture presented here represents a significant step toward realizing truly lossless data transmission over long distances, underpinned by the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics. Further research will focus on practical implementation challenges and exploring the scalability of this technology.

title: Meta-Learning for Automated Feature Engineering
abstract: This paper explores the application of meta-learning techniques to automate feature engineering, a critical and often time-consuming step in the development of machine learning models. The core argument is that meta-learning offers a novel approach to learning optimal feature representations, bypassing the need for manual design. We propose a framework where a meta-learner iteratively refines feature representations by learning from feedback provided across a diverse set of target tasks. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional feature engineering, which relies heavily on expert intuition and domain knowledge. The paper outlines the key components of this system, including the meta-learner architecture, the task distribution, and the feedback mechanism. We demonstrate, conceptually, how this framework could operate and highlight the potential advantages of automating this process, leading to improved model performance and reduced development time. The central goal is to create a system that can dynamically adapt to new datasets and tasks, ultimately achieving superior results compared to manually engineered features.

title: Neural Protocol Control via Program Synthesis (NCPAS)
abstract: This paper introduces Neural Protocol Control via Program Synthesis (NCPAS), a novel approach to program synthesis that leverages the power of neural networks to directly learn and control program execution. The core idea is to utilize a neural network to generate program code from high-level specifications and to dynamically adjust the program's execution path during runtime. This is achieved through reinforcement learning, where the network's internal structure and parameters are optimized to maximize code correctness and efficiency. NCPAS represents a significant departure from traditional program synthesis techniques, which often rely on complex rule-based systems and exhaustive search algorithms, resulting in significant performance bottlenecks. The proposed method offers the potential for more efficient and adaptive program generation, particularly in scenarios involving dynamic environments and complex specifications. The key contributions of this work are the direct mapping of specifications to code through neural networks and the dynamic control of program execution guided by learned neural policies. The system aims to bridge the gap between high-level specification and low-level code execution, offering a more intuitive and potentially more powerful approach to program synthesis.

title: Adaptive Program Evolution Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents an Adaptive Program Evolution Algorithm (APEA), a novel approach to automated program development. The core idea is to create an algorithm capable of autonomously evolving a program's code structure and execution flow based on its runtime behavior and performance metrics. The algorithm leverages a hybrid mechanism combining Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) to enable the program itself to act as an "individual," undergoing self-modification and self-optimization to adapt to a given target task. Unlike traditional approaches where a program is passively executed, APEA facilitates a truly adaptive programming paradigm, where the program actively learns and improves its own design. This paper outlines the key components of the APEA, including the representation of programs as evolutionary individuals, the fitness function based on performance, and the learning mechanisms employed by the RL component. The proposed method demonstrates the potential to generate effective solutions for complex optimization problems automatically.

title: Dynamic Time-Scale Adaptation for Bayesian Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic time-scale adaptation (DTSA) framework for Bayesian neural networks, designed to optimize learning rates and network complexity based on the inherent temporal dynamics of the data. Traditional Bayesian neural network architectures often lack this adaptive capability, leading to suboptimal performance. Our approach utilizes a feedback loop to continuously monitor network performance and dynamically adjust parameters, resulting in improved generalization and robustness. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through extensive experiments on a variety of time-series datasets, showcasing significant improvements in both accuracy and training speed. The core mechanism centers on a tailored learning rate adjustment strategy that leverages the observed temporal patterns within the data.

title: 基于多变量正态分布的神经网络 (MVNBN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Multi-Variate Normal Bayesian Network (MVNBN), a novel neural network architecture designed to effectively learn and predict complex data by leveraging the properties of multivariate normal distributions. The core concept involves representing the network's parameters as those of a multi-variate normal distribution. This allows the network to inherently capture correlations between variables, leading to improved performance in tasks such as classification and regression, particularly when dealing with datasets exhibiting non-independence. We demonstrate the theoretical underpinnings of MVNBN and outline its key components. The network's training process is based on maximizing the likelihood of the observed data given the learned multi-variate normal distributions. Experimental results, though not presented here due to the focus on the theoretical framework, would demonstrate the advantages of MVNBN over traditional neural networks in scenarios involving correlated data. The key contribution of this work is the integration of multi-variate normal distributions within a neural network framework, providing a more principled approach to modeling complex data dependencies.

title: Meta-Learning with Evolutionary Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces a novel meta-learning approach leveraging Evolutionary Recurrent Neural Networks (ERNNs) to address the limitations of conventional meta-learning algorithms. The core challenge in meta-learning is the generalization across diverse tasks, often failing when tasks exhibit significantly different distributions. Our proposed method utilizes an ERNN to dynamically optimize the parameters of a base learner. The ERNN itself is governed by an evolutionary algorithm, iteratively adapting its internal state to guide the learning process of the base learner. This creates a feedback loop where the evolutionary algorithm drives the recurrent network's adaptation, leading to enhanced robustness and generalization capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this combined approach through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, outlining a framework that promises more adaptable and reliable meta-learning systems. The key innovations lie in the synergistic combination of evolutionary computation and recurrent neural networks, creating a system that can effectively navigate highly variable task landscapes. Specifically, we propose a framework where the ERNN's recurrent connections allow it to capture temporal dependencies in the optimization process of the base learner, while the evolutionary algorithm provides a robust and efficient exploration strategy. This approach aims to overcome the limitations of traditional meta-learning methods that often rely on fixed or hand-crafted optimization strategies.

title: MAPFL: Modular Adaptive Personalised Federated Learning From Visual Sentiment to Physical Activity
abstract: ABSTRACT Human‐centric sensing tasks such as visual sentiment analysis and smartphone‐based human activity recognition (HAR) exhibit strong client heterogeneity from feature, label, and concept shifts. Among these, concept shift—how individual users interpret and generate human‐centric signals—is particularly challenging yet underexplored in federated learning. We propose MAPFL (Modular Adaptive Personalised Federated Learning), a personalised federated framework that performs encoder‐level personalisation while preserving standard communication. Each client model is decomposed into a shared encoder and a local classifier head, and equipped with both global and personalised encoders. A gradient‐aligned personalisation controller learns client‐specific mixing coefficients that adaptively balance the two encoders based on the alignment of their gradients, allowing each client to decide how much to share versus personalise at the representation level. This design supports both image‐ and sensor‐based tasks. On an affective‐computing benchmark built from three in‐the‐wild visual sentiment datasets (ARTphoto, ABSTRACT, PARA) and on a smartphone‐based HAR benchmark derived from UCI HAR, MAPFL improves AUC and accuracy by up to 3.3% over strong federated and personalised baselines and converges faster and more stably. These results show that gradient‐aligned encoder personalisation is an effective and practical mechanism for handling multi‐dimensional heterogeneity in human‐centric sensing.

title: Reasoning Beyond Transcription: Audio Language Models on Child Stuttering Speech
abstract: Child speech differs from adult speech in acoustics, prosody, and linguistic structures. Speech disfluencies (such as repetitions) further challenge automatic understanding. While Audio Language Models (ALMs) show strong semantic reasoning from speech audio, their ability to reason about disfluent child speech in mixed-speaker settings remains unexplored. We investigate this through two tasks: child-focused semantic summarization and speech entailment. title: Online Draft Co-Training for Speculative Decoding in Large-Scale, Long-Context RL Post-Training
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates rollout generation, which dominates the cost of reinforcement learning (RL) post-training. Online co-training can further increase the draft's accuracy, yielding greater speedups. However, scaling this approach to co-training on large models with long contexts poses two obstacles: (1) branch attention is unsupported by standard causal context-parallel (CP) implementations, and (2) target features span across pipeline-parallel (PP) stages. We address both with an end-to-end system for large-scale online draft co-training. For CP, we extend packed, load-balanced zigzag ring attention by merging rank-local branch attention with causal main-sequence attention. For PP, TapChannel transports intermediate target features across stages via a separate path, leaving the pipeline schedule unaffected. Experiments demonstrate that co-trained drafts closely track the policy baseline while delivering substantial rollout and end-to-end speedups across model scales up to 122B. Our CP design achieves strong scaling at 256K tokens with significant memory savings over prior work, and our PP transport incurs modest overhead. Code can be found at https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/RL/issues/3698.

title: Cyberbullying Detection Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques: A Review
authors: Dr. Mohammad Nasiruddin Sana Bano Khan
abstract: The explosive growth of social media has made cyberbullying a widespread and serious concern, particularly for adolescents and young adults, with documented links to anxiety, depression, and, in extreme cases, self-harm. Because manual moderation cannot scale to the volume of content generated every day, automated detection using machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) has become an active research area. This paper reviews the evolution of cyberbullying detection research, from early lexicon- and rule-based methods through classical supervised classifiers such as Naïve Bayes, Support Vector Machines, and Random Forest, to modern deep architectures including Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Networks, and transformer-based language models such as BERT. We summarise the typical detection pipeline, compare the strengths and weaknesses of the major algorithm families, catalogue commonly used public datasets, and discuss the open challenges that remain — including context and sarcasm understanding, multilingual and code-mixed text, multimodal (text-image-video) content, class imbalance, and real-time, cross-platform deployment. The review is intended to orient new researchers and practitioners toward promising directions for building more robust, fair, and scalable cyberbullying detection systems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Fluid Dynamics Simulation (QEDS)
abstract: Quantum-Enhanced Fluid Dynamics Simulation (QEDS) presents a novel approach to complex fluid dynamics simulation, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics to accelerate calculations and enhance the fidelity of results. Traditional CFD methods often struggle with computationally intensive scenarios, particularly those involving extreme conditions and high dimensionality. QEDS aims to overcome these limitations by integrating quantum effects into the simulation process. This paper explores the fundamental concepts behind QEDS, detailing the core mechanism for achieving enhanced performance, and discussing potential applications across diverse fluid dynamics domains.

title: Adaptive Information Entropy Theory
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Information Entropy Theory (AITE), a novel framework for data compression and analysis that leverages machine learning to dynamically adjust information entropy. Traditional entropy measures are often fixed and lack the flexibility to adapt to evolving data distributions. AITE employs a neural network to learn the relationship between data and entropy, enabling automated adjustment to optimize compression and analysis performance. This work addresses the limitations of static entropy models by providing a dynamic and intelligent approach to data representation and processing. We present a comprehensive evaluation of AITE, demonstrating its effectiveness in various data compression and analysis scenarios.

title: Self-Referential Program Synthesis via Formal Concept Theory
abstract: Current approaches to program synthesis often struggle with creating robust and maintainable code due to a lack of effective reasoning about the source code itself. This paper proposes a novel framework for self-referential program synthesis leveraging the principles of Formal Concept Theory (FCT). FCT provides a powerful way to represent programs as concepts, allowing for independent analysis of the program object and its associated properties. By establishing relationships between these concepts, we enable a synthesis process that inherently understands and validates the generated code based on its own structure and properties. This approach promises to move beyond brittle, rule-based synthesis towards more intelligent and reliable code generation, addressing a key limitation in existing program synthesis techniques. The core of the method involves creating concepts from program elements and then using these concepts to guide the synthesis process, ensuring that the resulting program aligns with its own design. We outline the theoretical foundation and present a conceptual framework for this system, highlighting its potential to improve the quality and maintainability of synthesized software.

title: Hyperdimensional Computing with Symbolic Representations
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to knowledge representation and reasoning by integrating hyperdimensional computing (HDC) with symbolic representations. HDC, characterized by its high-dimensional vector representations and efficient similarity search capabilities, offers a powerful engine for pattern recognition. However, HDC vectors themselves are devoid of inherent meaning. This work proposes a framework where HDC is leveraged for rapid similarity assessments, while symbolic representations provide the necessary context and semantic interpretation. The core idea is to use HDC vectors as features within a symbolic reasoning system, enabling a hybrid approach that combines the computational efficiency of HDC with the expressive power of symbolic logic. We detail the architecture of this system, focusing on the mapping between HDC vectors and symbolic concepts, and discuss potential applications in areas such as knowledge discovery, natural language understanding, and expert systems. The key contribution lies in establishing a systematic method for bridging the numerical and symbolic processing paradigms, opening up new avenues for intelligent systems.

title: 基于自适应量子纠缠的非线性几何优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to non-linear geometric optimization utilizing the principles of quantum entanglement. Traditional optimization algorithms often struggle with complex, high-dimensional spaces, particularly when dealing with non-convex problems. We introduce a new algorithm, termed "Quantum Geometric Optimization" (QGO), which leverages the unique properties of quantum entanglement to enhance the search process and achieve solutions that are significantly more robust and efficient than conventional methods. The core of QGO lies in the creation of a 'quantum-entangled search space' where the optimization landscape exhibits inherent non-linearity. By employing specific entanglement operations, we enable a novel approach to global search, surpassing the capabilities of existing algorithms. We demonstrate the effectiveness of QGO through the solution of a complex, high-dimensional linear programming problem, achieving a substantially improved solution compared to state-of-the-art algorithms. The core mechanism focuses on manipulating entanglement to induce a "structured search" that effectively explores the solution space. The results underscore the potential of quantum entanglement as a powerful tool for tackling challenging optimization problems.

title: Multi-Scale Symbolic Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Multi-Scale Symbolic Reasoning Engine designed to address the challenges of symbolic reasoning with heterogeneous data scales. The core concept is to decompose symbolic information into multiple scales and employ a layered architecture with dedicated reasoning modules for each scale. This facilitates information interaction and inference across different scales, ultimately leading to more accurate and efficient conclusions. The engine's key innovation lies in its ability to effectively manage and integrate information at varying granularities, a crucial factor often overlooked in traditional symbolic reasoning systems. We outline the engine's architecture, detailing the scale decomposition process and the corresponding reasoning modules. Furthermore, we explore potential applications and discuss future research directions.

title: Contextualized Memory Networks with Adaptive Attention Routing
abstract: This paper addresses the limitations of existing Memory Networks (MemNets) concerning their reliance on fixed-depth memory structures and their inability to dynamically prioritize relevant memory locations. We introduce a novel approach incorporating an adaptive attention routing mechanism within the MemNet architecture. This mechanism allows the network to learn and apply contextual relevance scores, effectively selecting and weighting memory locations during information retrieval. The core claim is that existing MemNets lack adaptive mechanisms for prioritizing relevant memory locations. The proposed method aims to optimize information retrieval efficiency by dynamically adjusting the attention weights, ultimately leading to improved performance in tasks requiring contextual understanding and memory access. Experimental results (simulated) demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptive attention routing in enhancing the network's ability to focus on pertinent memory locations, compared to a standard MemNet. The key innovation lies in the dynamic adjustment of attention, providing a more nuanced and context-aware approach to memory access.

title: Probability Logic Framework for Set Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel set optimization algorithm based on a probabilistic framework, leveraging the inherent redundancy and overlap within sets. The core idea is to transform the probabilistic concept of "probability" into a probabilistic model, incorporating "redundancy" and "overlap" to enable efficient optimization. We propose a dynamic probability model that adapts to system states, automatically adjusting probability parameters to guide the optimization process. This approach offers a more flexible and robust solution compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios characterized by complex non-linear relationships and uncertainty. The paper details the design of this framework, explores its application to a specific example, and discusses its potential for broader utilization in diverse optimization problems.

title: Information Entropy and Probability Distribution Adaptive Optimization
abstract: This paper explores the application of information entropy and probability distribution modeling to adaptive optimization of machine learning models. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter adjustments, limiting the model's ability to effectively adapt to evolving data distributions. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts the probability distribution of the model's parameters based on the observed data, maximizing the probability of the target variable. This adaptive approach enhances model generalization and robustness. The core mechanism involves employing information entropy to quantify uncertainty and probabilistic distributions to represent model parameters, allowing for a continuous, self-adjusting optimization process. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm through a series of experiments evaluating model performance on diverse datasets.

title: Fractal-Based Data Compression for Graph Representation
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to graph data compression utilizing fractal coding techniques. The core idea revolves around representing a graph as a sequence of fractal patterns, leveraging a learned fractal dimension parameter to manage the level of detail and consequently, achieve efficient compression ratios. Unlike traditional graph representations such as adjacency matrices or edge lists, this method exploits the inherent self-similarity often found in complex networks. The research demonstrates the potential for significant compression while retaining crucial structural characteristics of the graph. The method offers a promising alternative for scenarios where graph storage and transmission are critical challenges. The key contributions lie in the application of fractal coding specifically to graph data, and the development of a learned fractal dimension parameter to control the compression process. The theoretical framework and the proposed method are presented, along with an analysis of the compression performance.

title: Dynamic Topological Information Coding (DTIC)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topological Information Coding (DTIC), a novel approach to neural network architecture design that moves beyond traditional weight-based optimization. The core claim is that the topology of a neural network can be dynamically encoded and optimized. This is achieved through a mechanism leveraging differential geometry and topological field theory, mapping network connection weights to curvature and tensor fields. Gradient descent is then utilized to optimize these topological fields, resulting in an adaptive and self-organizing network architecture. Unlike existing methods that treat topology as fixed or indirectly influence it through weight training, DTIC directly optimizes the topological field, offering a fundamentally new approach to neural network design. The key contribution lies in the explicit control and adaptation of network connectivity based on topological properties, potentially leading to more efficient and performant networks. This work presents a theoretical framework and a proposed methodology for realizing this dynamic topology optimization.

title: Title: Bayesian Stochastic Differential Equations with Adaptive Kernel Selection
abstract: This paper presents a novel Bayesian framework for Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) that leverages an adaptive kernel selection strategy. Traditional SDE models often employ static, predetermined kernels, hindering their ability to effectively model complex systems and achieve optimal predictive performance. This work introduces a Bayesian neural network (BNN) architecture trained to dynamically select and adapt kernel functions based on the current data distribution. The BNN learns the optimal kernel for each SDE instance, continuously updating it as new data arrives. The core mechanism focuses on enhancing predictive accuracy and robustness through this adaptive kernel selection process. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations and experiments, showcasing significant improvements in model performance compared to traditional methods and fixed kernel approaches. The paper concludes with a discussion of the key findings and potential future directions.

title: On the Recall Scaling Laws in Mamba: A Theoretical and Mechanistic Study via Hashing
abstract: Associative Recall (AR) is the cognitive ability to learn and retrieve links between items in memory. In NLP, AR is used as a benchmark for evaluating the in-context memory capacity of architectures such as Mamba, and has been found to strongly correlate with language modeling performance. This paper explores AR from the perspective of mechanistic interpretability, aiming to reverse-engineer the exact internal algorithm used by Mamba to perform recall. Our key insight is that Mamba performs recall by implicitly learning linear hash functions, and we identify the low-level circuit that enables this behavior. Building on these findings and inspired by theoretical tools in similarity-preserving hashing, such as the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma, we develop a theoretical framework for analyzing AR, which we term Recall Scaling Laws. Given the vocabulary size and the number of facts in context, this framework allows us to (1) predict the embedding and state dimensions required for Mamba to achieve perfect recall, (2) predict recall success probability given the model dimensions, and (3) analyze multi-layer models and multi-head SSM patterns. Empirical results show that our theoretical findings are accurate and predictive, offering insights into how AR capacity scales with vocabulary, state, embedding size, and architecture.

title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
abstract: Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-$R_{ZZ}$ decomposition. In the simulations, bit-flip noise produces the larger degradation in the performance of the quantum optimization. The asymmetry is most visible in the layer-level and native-$R_{ZZ}$ simulations. We explain this by how the errors affect mixing, final measurements, and how they propagate inside the circuit. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This demonstrates that error-correction resources should be assigned not only according to physical error rates, but also according to how strongly each error channel affects the application. As a result, asymmetric quantum error correction proves useful even in cases where the noise model is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.

title: Beyond Sparse Rewards: A New Benchmark and Structure-Aware Graph Alignment for Micro-Drama Understanding
abstract: Micro-dramas, characterized by ultra-short durations and hyper-dense storylines, pose unique challenges for video understanding that conventional benchmarks fail to address. To bridge this gap, we introduce M-Drama, the first large-scale bilingual benchmark for micro-drama comprehension, featuring over 35K instances across 9,138 clips. Furthermore, while reinforcement learning can enhance VLMs on complex narratives, existing reward metrics often suffer from sparse and superficial signals, failing to capture intricate character identities and temporal structures. We propose SAGA (Structure-Aware Graph Alignment), a novel graph-matching reward function that models narratives as heterogeneous graphs. SAGA computes dense, rigorous rewards via decoupled semantic triplet and structural temporal matching. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct demonstrate that SAGA outperforms existing baselines, delivering substantial improvements in open-ended accuracy and summary quality, while maintaining competitive out-of-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/qyx1121/MDrama_SAGA.

title: Importance-driven Safety and Performance Testing for Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: In many Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems, the decisions of a trained policy differ in their impact on the policy’s expected safety and performance. Testing should therefore focus on states in which the agent’s decisions have the greatest influence on these outcomes. We extend a recently proposed approach for testing RL agents in states that are most relevant to safety to the joint evaluation of safety and performance. Our method rigorously computes a ranking of state importance with respect to both objectives across the state space. At each iteration, the testing framework derives optimistic and pessimistic estimates of safety and performance, which provide lower and upper bounds on the expected outcomes of policy execution across all modeled states. Upon convergence, the approach partitions the state space into regions according to whether the specified safety or performance properties are satisfied, thereby providing insights into the policy’s weaknesses. Ourapproach is characterized by two key properties. (1) Optimal Test-Case Selection: at any point during the testing process, the policy is evaluated in the states that are most critical for assessing safety and performance. (2) Formal Guarantees: by evaluating the policy in only a fraction of the state space, our approach nevertheless provides formal verification guarantees over the entire modeled state space. We provide a detailed evaluation on several examples, demonstrating that our method identifies unsafe and suboptimal policy behavior with low testing effort.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum trajectory planning algorithm leveraging the unique properties of quantum states to enhance path exploration and optimization. Traditional path-finding algorithms rely on classical computation, but this approach utilizes quantum mechanics to achieve significantly improved efficiency in this domain. The core mechanism involves transforming path exploration into a quantum computation, and employing quantum algorithms to guide the search towards optimal paths. The paper presents a detailed explanation of the algorithm's design, its mathematical foundations, and its potential benefits for various trajectory planning scenarios.

The core mechanism involves an iterative refinement process, driven by the stochastic nature of the matrix, to achieve a more robust and adaptable optimization. This research offers a promising alternative for enhancing machine learning models, particularly in situations where data dynamics are significant.

title: Non-Linear Chaos Algorithm: Quantum Acceleration
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum computing to accelerate the notoriously complex process of chaos theory. We propose a novel non-linear chaos algorithm, leveraging quantum principles to simplify computational steps and significantly enhance performance compared to classical approaches. The core mechanism centers around the application of a tailored quantum algorithm designed to address the inherent limitations of traditional chaos simulation. We demonstrate, through simulations and preliminary analysis, that this quantum-enhanced approach offers a substantial improvement in computational speed and the ability to explore higher dimensional chaos spaces, ultimately paving the way for more sophisticated analysis and potentially groundbreaking discoveries within the field of chaos dynamics. The study also highlights the conceptual implications of quantum acceleration and its potential impact on the future of chaotic system research.

title: Meta-Learning for Algorithm Adaptive Adjustment
abstract: This paper investigates the application of meta-learning techniques to enable algorithm adaptive adjustment. Traditional algorithms often struggle with adapting to novel environments or tasks, requiring manual tuning or retraining. Meta-learning offers a promising solution by allowing algorithms to learn *how* to learn, effectively enabling them to quickly adapt to new situations. This work explores the core claim that meta-learning facilitates algorithmic adaptation and details the core mechanism of leveraging meta-learning algorithms trained on diverse, related tasks to optimize parameters or structure for new tasks. The research focuses on the automated and efficient adjustment of algorithms, addressing a significant challenge in dynamic and unpredictable environments. We present a framework for utilizing meta-learning to achieve rapid adaptation, outlining key considerations and potential benefits.

title: Quantum Clock Geometry Complexity
abstract: Quantum Clock Geometry Complexity explores the application of geometric complexity to enhance the precision and stability of quantum computation. Current quantum computing architectures, while promising, face significant challenges in achieving fault-tolerant operation due to inherent quantum decoherence. This research proposes a novel algorithm that leverages geometric complexity to dynamically adjust the quantum system's internal parameters, thereby mitigating these decoherence effects and ultimately improving the fidelity of quantum computations. The core mechanism centers around a sophisticated mapping function that iteratively refines the geometric complexity of the quantum clock, optimizing for specific quantum algorithms. This revised clock, governed by the defined geometric complexity, results in a more robust and accurate system.

title: Memory-Augmented Graph Neural Networks for Long-Range Dependencies
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, a significant limitation of standard GNNs is their difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies within graphs. This challenge stems primarily from the vanishing gradient problem, where gradients diminish as they propagate through multiple layers during training, hindering the network's ability to effectively learn relationships between distant nodes. This paper proposes a novel approach – Memory-Augmented Graph Neural Networks (MAGNNs) – to address this limitation. MAGNNs augment a standard GNN architecture with an external memory module. This memory module acts as a repository for information extracted from distant nodes, allowing the network to maintain and retrieve relevant contextual information regardless of spatial distance. We introduce a detailed framework for MAGNNs, outlining the memory architecture, the integration process with the GNN, and the training strategy. Experimental results on several benchmark graph datasets demonstrate that MAGNNs significantly outperform standard GNNs in tasks requiring the modeling of long-range dependencies, validating the efficacy of our approach.

title: 基于量子纠缠的自适应时间尺度调控
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to time scale control based on quantum entanglement, offering a fundamentally different method compared to traditional techniques. We propose a system of quantum entanglement manipulation that allows for precise modeling of complex systems by dynamically adjusting the properties of entangled states. The core of our methodology lies in leveraging the inherent self-adaptative nature of quantum entanglement to achieve a level of control previously unattainable with classical approaches. This allows for a detailed understanding of how the system's temporal dynamics are influenced by subtle environmental factors. The proposed method exhibits significant potential for advancing the field of complex systems modeling, particularly in scenarios requiring high precision and responsiveness.

title: Dynamic Probability Space Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic probability space learning framework designed to enhance model accuracy through adaptive probability distribution adjustment based on observed data. Traditional probabilistic models often lack this dynamic capability, limiting their predictive power. Our approach leverages neural networks to learn the probability distributions of the model, continuously refining them as new data arrives. This dynamic adjustment allows the model to better represent the underlying data distribution, resulting in improved performance on a variety of tasks. The core mechanism centers around a feedback loop that iteratively updates the probability distributions based on observed outcomes. The framework demonstrates significant improvements in forecasting accuracy and robustness compared to static probability models.

title: Title: Topology-Based Machine Learning for Data Clustering
abstract: Topology-based machine learning offers a novel approach to data clustering, moving beyond traditional distance-based methods by explicitly incorporating topological information. This paper investigates the potential of utilizing graph-based clustering algorithms enhanced with topological invariants to achieve superior clustering accuracy. We propose a framework where the inherent structure of data clusters—defined by their connectivity and balance—is exploited to guide the clustering process. This paper details the development of a new clustering algorithm, leveraging graph theory and topological concepts, with a focus on improving cluster coherence and reducing noise. The core mechanism centers on incorporating connectivity measures and balance conditions into the graph construction and evaluation phases of the algorithm. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through comprehensive experimental results, showcasing significant improvements in clustering performance compared to existing techniques.

title: Based on Quantum Entanglement: A Distributed Time Synchronization Protocol
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed time synchronization protocol leveraging quantum entanglement. The core claim is that absolute time synchronization, surpassing the limitations of classical physics, is achievable through the utilization of entangled particles, eliminating the need for a global time reference. The protocol centers on a mechanism for precise time calibration using entangled states, capitalizing on the inherent coherence of entangled states to perform absolute measurements of time differences and achieve synchronization. This approach fundamentally overcomes the reliance on global reference frames inherent in traditional time synchronization methods, offering a quantum mechanical solution to the problem. The protocol details the key steps involved, focusing on the generation, distribution, and measurement of entangled particles to establish a synchronized time base across spatially separated nodes. This research contributes to the emerging field of quantum time synchronization and its potential applications in precision timing, distributed sensing, and fundamental physics experiments.

title: 基于自适应的神经网络的梯度下降算法
abstract: This paper investigates a novel gradient descent algorithm incorporating adaptive learning rates. Traditional gradient descent suffers from limitations in convergence, particularly when dealing with complex, non-convex loss landscapes. This work proposes a dynamic learning rate adjustment mechanism to address these limitations, optimizing parameter updates for improved model performance. The proposed algorithm leverages a feedback loop that continuously assesses the gradient's magnitude and magnitude squared, adjusting the learning rate accordingly. This adaptive approach mitigates the risk of oscillations and ensures a more stable convergence path. The research explores the effectiveness of this dynamic learning rate adjustment through rigorous analysis and validation on a range of neural network architectures. The paper concludes with a detailed description of the algorithm's implementation and the results demonstrating its superior performance compared to standard gradient descent and other adaptive optimization techniques.
