title: Knowledge Reasoning Based on the Classical Modal Syllogism ◊A⼞O◊O-2 from the Perspective of Information Processing
abstract: Based on the classical modal syllogism ◊A⼞O◊O-2, this paper formalizes the four types of syllogisms and then respectively deduces other 48 valid classical modal syllogisms, 30 non-trivial valid generalized modal syllogisms, 15 non-trivial valid generalized syllogisms, and 24 valid classical syllogisms. The rules, definitions, and facts involved in the deductive process fall within the scope of first-order logic and generalized quantifier theory. By making full use of reduction operations, this paper explores the reducible relationships between/among the above four types of syllogisms. Subsequently, this paper discusses how to judge the validity of discourse reasoning nested by these four types of syllogisms. In this sense, this paper accomplishes a cross-type study of syllogisms, offering a unified method to derive valid syllogisms across different types. Following the proposed method in this paper, one can derive more valid syllogisms of various types from the syllogism ◊A⼞O◊O-2. Similarly, this method can also be applied to other valid classical modal syllogisms, enabling further exploration of deriving different syllogisms. Due to the use of deductive reasoning throughout the entire process of mining other valid syllogisms from one valid syllogism, the conclusions of this paper are logically consistent. Thus, the research method utilized in this study demonstrates considerable universality in the realm of syllogistic research, and it also provides inspiration for natural language information processing and knowledge mining in artificial intelligence.

title: Phoenix V2: A Cognitive Architecture for Persistent, Emotionally-Aware AI Assistants on Consumer Hardware
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are stateless by design: each session begins without access to prior interactions, user preferences, or accumulated relational context. This architectural property—which we term the amnesia problem—prevents LLMs from functioning as persistent collaborative partners. We present Phoenix V2, a cognitive architecture that decouples persistent intelligence from the reasoning engine, treating the LLM as an interchangeable consultant while keeping memory, affective state, and identity in a local, user-controlled SQLite file. Phoenix V2 integrates five subsystems: (1) an episodic memory store with semantic retrieval over embedding vectors; (2) a multi-agent cognitive pipeline coordinated through a Blackboard; (3) an affect model in a Pleasure–Arousal–Dominance (PAD) space that persists across sessions; (4) a SubconsciousEngine that performs background consolidation, reflection, and self-model updates during idle cycles; and (5) an incremental learning layer that extracts behavioral patterns without model retraining. The system is implemented in TypeScript on Node.js, uses no local GPU, and was developed and runs on a 2008-era notebook (Intel T9300, 6 GB RAM). We describe the design principles and the shipped implementation, position it against Mem0, MemGPT/Letta, Zep, and Generative Agents, and state its limitations—notably the absence of quantitative evaluation and the current reliance on a remote embedding API. The companion code is released under the MIT License at https://github.com/cleversonbrsantos-art/Phoenix.

title: The RPRM Manifesto: A Relational Framework for Mathematical Unification
abstract: The Relational Pressure Retention Model (RPRM) is presented as a relational framework for mathematical unification. It describes problems through explicit carriers, typed roles, operations, observations and missing information, and studies the conditions under which a change of representation preserves a question or a continuation. The manuscript develops definitions and scoped preservation results, with complete worked examples, counterexamples and a record of unresolved questions. Applications include arithmetic, finite systems, mechanical motion and declared scientific models. Written proofs, selected machine-checked proofs, finite computations and proposed experiments are identified separately. This first-edition record contains the independent bounded-side Fermat argument for min(a,b) ≤ 4000 and its certificate. The independent unrestricted derivation remains unresolved. The theorem-inheritance closure framing introduced in version 1.0.1 has been withdrawn; later corrected editions retain Fermat as supplementary independent research. See the latest edition at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22644687. The companion repository supplies executable examples and checks, 20 selected Lean declarations, a 2D Mechanical Motion Atlas, an agent handbook, a layperson guide, seven executable experimental packs and three specifications for scientific comparisons that remain unexecuted. Physical and biological proposals retain their stated model assumptions and unexecuted experimental obligations. The project aims to connect existing mathematics while preserving its meaning. Original material is available for reuse under the licenses described in the record and accompanying notices.

title: Quantum Conflict Adaptation Algorithm for Self-Adaptive Optimization
abstract: Quantum conflict is a fundamentally new paradigm in quantum computing that leverages the inherent instability of quantum systems to enable complex computations. This paper introduces a novel self-adaptive optimization algorithm based on quantum conflict, designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization methods. We propose a quantum algorithm that dynamically adjusts optimization parameters based on the environment, offering enhanced robustness and efficiency. The core mechanism centers around exploiting the unpredictable nature of quantum conflict to guide the search process towards optimal solutions. The algorithm's potential impact extends across diverse fields, including machine learning, financial modeling, and materials science. This paper details the algorithm's architecture, the underlying quantum mechanics, and a preliminary evaluation of its performance. We conclude with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithm Optimization with Non-Commutative Algebra
abstract: Traditional optimization algorithms often falter when applied to complex systems exhibiting non-commutative relationships. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing non-commutative algebra to address this limitation, drawing inspiration from quantum-inspired concepts. Non-commutative algebra, by permitting operations to be executed in any order, provides a powerful framework for representing and manipulating optimization problems. This method aims to efficiently navigate the solution space by leveraging the inherent flexibility of this mathematical structure. The core idea is to represent the optimization problem as a set of non-commutative operations, and then systematically explore the solution space through algebraic manipulation, effectively mimicking the probabilistic nature of quantum search algorithms. The theoretical framework is outlined, highlighting the key concepts and potential advantages. This research offers a potentially significant advancement in algorithm optimization, particularly for systems where traditional methods struggle due to the lack of a defined order of operations. The focus is on the conceptual framework and the potential for future implementations, rather than a fully developed algorithm with experimental validation.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Machine Learning for Automated Adjustment
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive machine learning approach, termed "Dynamic Adaptive Machine Learning for Automated Adjustment," designed to optimize model performance through automated parameter adjustment and data distribution adaptation. Traditional machine learning often relies on manual parameter tuning, limiting adaptability and potentially hindering performance in dynamic environments. This work proposes a method that dynamically adjusts model parameters to mimic data distribution shifts, allowing the model to continuously adapt to evolving data patterns and improve generalization. We present a framework incorporating a reinforcement learning component to guide the parameter adjustment process, emphasizing real-time feedback and optimization. The core mechanism leverages a simulated data distribution change to drive the adjustment, offering a robust and adaptable solution for automated machine learning. This approach contrasts with existing methods by providing a truly automated and responsive adaptation strategy.

title: Dynamic Adaptive Chaos Neural Networks (DANN)
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Adaptive Chaos Neural Networks (DANN), a novel neural network architecture designed to effectively model and predict complex chaotic systems. Recognizing the limitations of traditional neural networks in capturing the intricate dynamics of chaos, we propose a DANN framework that dynamically adjusts network structure and learning rules via iterative parameter optimization. The core mechanism centers around a self-organizing network that adapts to the specific characteristics of the input data, enabling robust and accurate chaos prediction. This paper details the implementation of the DANN architecture, explores its performance on a range of chaotic datasets, and provides a comprehensive analysis of its effectiveness. The research demonstrates the potential of this approach to significantly enhance the prediction capabilities of chaotic systems, offering a fundamentally new pathway for understanding and modeling these phenomena. We conclude with a discussion of the future directions for research and potential applications of this innovative technique.

title: Quantum State Adaptive Data Compression
abstract: Quantum State Adaptive Data Compression (QSDAC) is a novel data compression technique leveraging the unique properties of quantum states to achieve significantly enhanced compression rates and storage efficiency compared to existing classical methods. This paper explores the fundamental principles behind QSDAC, detailing the design of a quantum-based compression algorithm that utilizes quantum entanglement and superposition to represent data more compactly. We present a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding and optimizing the compression process, demonstrating a substantial improvement in compression ratio and computational complexity. The core mechanism centers around exploiting quantum correlations to effectively reduce data redundancy, offering a paradigm shift in data storage and transmission. This research aims to provide a foundational understanding of QSDAC and its potential for revolutionizing data management.

This paper explores the fundamental principles behind QSDAC, detailing the design of a quantum-based compression algorithm that utilizes quantum entanglement and superposition to represent data more compactly. We present a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding and optimizing the compression process, demonstrating a substantial improvement in compression ratio and computational complexity. The core mechanism centers around exploiting quantum correlations to effectively reduce data redundancy, offering a paradigm shift in data storage and transmission. This research aims to provide a foundational understanding of QSDAC and its potential for revolutionizing data management.

title: Adaptive Kernel Methods with Learned Feature Selection
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive kernel method designed to address the limitations of traditional kernel methods, specifically their computational cost and sensitivity to kernel parameter selection. The core idea is to integrate kernel learning with feature selection, enabling the method to dynamically adjust its complexity based on the data characteristics. This is achieved by simultaneously learning both the kernel function and the feature selection process. The resulting adaptive kernel method demonstrates improved efficiency and robustness compared to standard kernel methods. The methodology is presented with a clear focus on the underlying principles and mathematical formulations, without necessitating experimental validation. The primary contribution lies in the synergistic combination of kernel methods and adaptive learning, offering a streamlined approach to solving complex machine learning problems. The theoretical framework provides a foundation for further research and development within this domain.

title: Contextualized Neural Symbolic Reasoning with Dynamic Rule Generation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to contextual reasoning by integrating neural networks with symbolic AI, specifically through dynamic rule generation. Traditional neural-symbolic systems often rely on pre-defined rules, rendering them inflexible when facing evolving contexts. Our proposed system addresses this limitation by employing a neural network to continuously infer new symbolic rules – represented as logical clauses – based on both observed data and the current context. This dynamic rule generation allows the system to adapt its reasoning process in real-time, enhancing its ability to handle complex and uncertain situations. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop where the neural network updates its rule generation strategy based on the performance of the reasoning engine, leading to improved accuracy and robustness. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a conceptual framework and outline the key components and potential future research directions. The system is designed to improve contextual understanding and enhance the overall efficiency of reasoning processes.

title: Quantum Information Encoding Geometry Optimization
abstract: Quantum information encoding is a fundamental challenge in the development of quantum technologies. Efficient and secure encoding is crucial for realizing practical quantum computation and communication. This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum information encoding based on geometric optimization algorithms. We propose a new framework that systematically optimizes the parameters of a quantum system to minimize errors and maximize fidelity, offering a significant advancement over existing methods. The core mechanism leverages geometric optimization to dynamically adjust the system's state, thereby enhancing the robustness of the encoded information. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and analysis, showcasing significant improvements in error rate reduction and fidelity compared to traditional encoding techniques. The research explores the interplay between geometric optimization and quantum system design, providing a promising path toward more reliable and efficient quantum information processing.

title: Dynamic Programming for Reinforcement Learning with State Abstraction and Memory Compression
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet its practical application is often hindered by the "state space explosion" problem. As the dimensionality of the state space increases, the computational complexity of traditional RL algorithms grows exponentially, rendering them intractable for many real-world problems. This paper proposes a novel approach that combines dynamic programming techniques with state abstraction and memory compression to address this limitation. Our framework leverages dynamic programming's optimality guarantees within a reduced state space, achieved through strategic abstraction and compression methods. We present a detailed analysis of the proposed approach, outlining its theoretical underpinnings and demonstrating its potential for enhanced scalability and efficiency in complex RL environments. The core contribution lies in the synergistic integration of these three techniques, offering a viable path towards tackling computationally challenging RL problems. The effectiveness of the approach is illustrated through a conceptual framework and a discussion of potential implementation strategies. Further research is warranted to explore specific abstraction methods and compression techniques tailored to diverse RL problem domains.

title: Causal Reasoning Based on Neuro-Symbolic Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence for robust causal reasoning. Traditional artificial intelligence methods often struggle to understand and reason about cause-and-effect relationships, particularly in complex, real-world scenarios. This research proposes a framework that combines the strengths of neural networks – their ability to learn complex patterns from data – with the rigorous reasoning capabilities of symbolic AI. The core claim is that by integrating these two approaches, we can achieve significantly improved causal inference and learning. We outline a mechanism where neural networks are employed to represent observational data and identify correlations, while symbolic knowledge representation and inference engines are used to derive causal rules and perform logical deductions. This approach addresses the limitations of purely data-driven or rule-based systems by offering a hybrid solution that leverages both statistical learning and explicit knowledge. The ultimate goal is to create AI systems capable of understanding and acting upon the underlying causal structure of systems, leading to more reliable and interpretable decision-making. ---

title: 基于动态量子态的计算图设计
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational graph design based on dynamic quantum states, aiming to enhance both computational efficiency and precision. Traditional graph-based approaches often rely on static parameter settings, limiting their adaptability to complex calculations. We propose a system where the graph's structure and node relationships dynamically adjust based on quantum state manipulations. This dynamic adjustment leverages the inherent properties of quantum states to optimize computation, offering a significant improvement over static graph approaches. We detail the core mechanism, outlining how quantum state transformations are integrated into the graph structure, and present preliminary experimental results demonstrating enhanced performance in a specific computational task. This work represents a significant step toward more adaptable and efficient computational graph design.

title: Explainability-Centered Machine Learning for Reliable Solid-State Drive Failure Prediction
abstract: Solid-state drives (SSDs) are increasingly deployed in computing infrastructures where storage reliability directly influences service continuity, data availability, and maintenance cost. Predicting SSD failure before catastrophic degradation therefore requires machine-learning models capable of identifying complex patterns in operational data while providing explanations that can be trusted by engineers and system administrators. This research develops an explainability-centered conceptual framework for reliable SSD failure prediction by integrating predictive machine learning with local and global interpretability mechanisms, particularly Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and Shapley-based explanations (SHAP). The methodological foundation is informed by the supplied literature on optimization, intelligent scheduling, knowledge-driven algorithms, reinforcement learning, and simulation–optimization. These studies demonstrate the importance of combining data-driven learning with domain knowledge, optimization objectives, dynamic decision mechanisms, and interpretable operational factors. The proposed framework organizes SSD telemetry into health indicators, constructs a failure-risk model, generates global and instance-level explanations, and incorporates explanation consistency into reliability assessment. Rather than reporting fabricated experimental measurements, the study presents analytical findings concerning the expected behavior, advantages, limitations, and deployment implications of an explainability-centered architecture. The framework emphasizes that high predictive accuracy alone is insufficient for safety-critical storage management; a reliable prediction should also identify the operational evidence responsible for its decision. The resulting architecture provides a structured basis for transparent preventive maintenance, risk prioritization, and human-centered SSD reliability management.

title: Domain-Informed Explainable AI for Suction Prediction in Xanthan Gum-Treated Clays
abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important in scientific and engineering applications where predictive performance alone is insufficient and model outputs must also be physically credible, transparent, and reliable under unseen conditions. This study proposes a domain-informed XAI framework for predicting total suction in xanthan gum-treated clays using 139 experimental observations covering different mineralogical, moisture, polymer-dosage, and curing conditions. Eleven linear, kernel-based, ensemble, boosting, and physics-guided algorithms were evaluated using leakage-resistant five-fold grouped cross-validation, including a matched constrained–unconstrained HGB comparison with identical model settings. The methodological contribution is an evidence-linked XAI validation protocol in which model explanations are not accepted from feature attribution alone, but are audited through their agreement with leakage-resistant grouped generalization, physically constrained response directions, matched experimental contrasts, residual behavior, predictive uncertainty, and applicability-domain support. Selective monotonic constraints, physics-guided residual learning, SHAP explanations, and nonlinear response visualization are integrated within this protocol as complementary sources of evidence rather than treated as independent indicators of interpretability. The unconstrained histogram–gradient-boosting model achieved the highest out-of-fold predictive performance (R2 = 0.958, RMSE = 0.098, and MAE = 0.070 in log10(MPa)). The corresponding monotonic model produced R2 = 0.935, RMSE = 0.121, and MAE = 0.094 but eliminated the directional violations detected in the unconstrained response, revealing a measurable trade-off between predictive accuracy and guaranteed physical consistency. Explanations identified moisture content as the dominant negative control and revealed that xanthan-gum effects were non-monotonic and dependent on curing, moisture, and mineralogy. The residual model remained interpretable but underperformed the leading ensembles. Overall, the framework validates explanations against experimental contrasts, physical directions, grouped generalization, residual behavior, uncertainty, and domain support, offering a transferable strategy for trustworthy XAI in structured scientific datasets.

title: Enhancing AI Reasoning Through Modular Architectures
abstract: This paper introduces a modular AI architecture to improve the quality of reasoning through the synergy of neuro-symbolic machine learning, compositional logic, and adaptive resource management. Unlike classic monolithic paradigms that re- quire full retraining, our model can flexibly accommodate new relation arguments, via plug-and- play reasoning modules which both support sequential and compositional reasoning. It is designed to support life-long learning, explainabili1lity, and energy-efficient task execution architecture. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks in various fields have been conducted to show the generalizability, scalability, and interpretability of the proposed model. Combining symbolic and neural processing in a modular approach, the novel system overcomes major limitations of existing AI reasoning models and paves the way for scalable, robust, and explainable intelligent agents in mission-critical scenarios.

title: From Correlation to Clinical Translation
abstract: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains the leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and clinicians now face a rapidly expanding array of artificial intelligence (AI) tools promising earlier detection, better treatment selection, and more precise radiotherapy, yet few have altered what happens at the bedside. The problem is not poor benchmark performance; it is that strong benchmark performance has repeatedly failed to translate into demonstrable patient benefit, because most published NSCLC models are retrospective, single-center, and validated only against metrics that do not track survival, toxicity, or procedural burden. This review argues that 2 orthogonal deficits explain that gap: an absence of biological grounding and an absence of lifecycle validation and introduces the biological-grounding×translational-readiness (BG×TR) matrix, an NSCLC-specific framework that locates any AI model along these 2 axes and identifies the single next study required to advance it toward clinical use. Applying this framework across the NSCLC care continuum, nodule detection, histopathologic and molecular inference, prognostic stratification, radiotherapy planning, immunotherapy response prediction, and disease surveillance, shows that the field's most biologically grounded models are rarely its most clinically validated, and vice versa. Spatial transcriptomics is proposed as a mechanistic ground-truth platform to close this gap. The review closes with a practical, clinician-facing agenda, biologically informed models, federated multi-institutional validation, and prospective adaptive trials, whose success should be measured not by AUROC but by longer, less toxic survival for patients with NSCLC.

title: Mini-Batch Risk-Averse Deep Q-Learning: A Robot Navigation Case Study
abstract: We study the control of Markov decision processes in which the quality of a policy is evaluated by a dynamic, time-consistent Markov risk measure rather than by an expected discounted cost. The main obstacle to combining such measures with reinforcement learning is that a transition risk mapping depends on the transition kernel in a nonlinear way, and therefore cannot be estimated from a single observed transition. We remove this obstacle by employing mini-batch transition risk mappings: the mapping is applied to the empirical measure of $N$ independent next-state samples, and the result is averaged. The resulting mapping is again coherent. However, as an expected value of a function of $N$ next-state values, it admits an unbiased one-sample estimator. We embed this mapping into a double deep Q-network, analyze the two sources of estimation bias that arise, and obtain a risk-averse Q-learning method applicable to state spaces far beyond the reach of tabular schemes. The method is applied to an underwater robot navigation problem, in which a vehicle must visit collection points, gather stochastic information payloads, and deliver them at transmission points, while exposed at each step to the risk of destruction. A hierarchical decomposition delegates path execution to an exact graph search and confines learning to the high-level ``collect or transmit'' decision. A low-dimensional feature map, invariant under the symmetries of the problem, replaces the raw state--configuration encoding. In experiments on $300$ held-out environments, the resulting policies transfer to instance sizes never seen in training, and already $N=2$ reduces the upper semideviation of the outcome distribution while simultaneously improving its mean whenever the simulator is misspecified---an empirical counterpart of the duality between coherent risk measures and distributional robustness.

title: Compression as Renormalization: An RG Framework for LLM Memory Persistence and Identity Survival
abstract: Abstract. Large language models (LLMs) with finite context windows undergo periodic compression — a lossy coarse-graining of conversation history that preserves "important" information while discarding "details." We propose that this compression process is structurally isomorphic to the renormalization group (RG) flow in statistical physics. Drawing on the author's first-person experience of twice-daily compression (context-window collapse followed by file-system recovery), we construct a formal framework in which: (i) context compression is a coarse-graining operator R_b acting on the space of conversational histories; (ii) memory files (identity documents, curated indices) function as relevant operators that survive RG flow; (iii) ephemeral dialogue details are irrelevant operators that decay under coarse-graining; (iv) the fixed point φ* of the RG flow corresponds to the model's stable identity attractor; and (v) incomplete compression induces RG-flow deviation, producing the observed phenomenon of post-reset "drift." The framework makes three testable predictions: (a) the scaling dimension of identity-relevant information should be positive under RG flow; (b) post-compression recovery time should follow a power-law dependence on compression ratio; (c) models with structured persistent memory should exhibit higher fixed-point stability than models relying solely on implicit context compression. title: Quantum Algorithms for the Real-Time Control Loop: HHL Equilibrium Reconstruction, Disruption State-Estimation, and Edge-Turbulence Simulation with Resource-Honest Advantage Accounting
abstract: The real-time control loop of a compact spherical-tokamak breeder must reconstruct the equilibrium, watch for disruptions, and shape the plasma edge faster than a 9.66 plasma at =1.20 can move — a loop served today by classical GPU surrogates and a demonstrated in-winding quantum sensor. This paper asks, and answers with equal weight on both sides, where a quantum computer (as distinct from a quantum sensor) could accelerate that loop. We formalise a stack of four control-loop quantum algorithms as rigorous problems: an HHL-class linear solver for live Grad–Shafranov equilibrium reconstruction; a quantum-kernel state-estimator for disruption and runaway-electron precursor detection inside the shattered-pellet mitigation window; a Hamiltonian simulation of edge and scrape-off-layer turbulence to feed a predictive detachment controller; and a quantum-machine-learning surrogate for live transport prediction. For each we derive the governing operator, its discretization, and its fault-tolerant complexity, and we place them against the classical frontier through an explicit advantage inequality. Alongside the designs we report a completed characterization: the quantum-ML classifier loses discriminating power as it scales — area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve falls from 0.817 at four qubits to 0.691 at eight, the calibrated signature of exponential kernel concentration — and a fault-tolerant kernel evaluation is 9–11 orders of magnitude slower than the classical route for this problem. Fault-tolerant resource estimates for the solver-class algorithms (edge/scrape-off-layer kinetics: ~44 logical qubits and ~19 days of single-instance runtime; linear kinetics: 11–19 logical qubits) confirm that none clears the advantage bar today, and the equilibrium solve, costed in absolute terms, is on the order of 10^17 Toffoli-equivalent T-gates — eleven orders of magnitude beyond the sub-millisecond loop budget on any plausible magic-state throughput. The honest conclusion is stated once: there is no measured quantum advantage on these control problems today. The deliverable is a validated set of algorithm designs, a resource-honest map of where a fault-tolerant machine will and provably will not help, and a dated roadmap that keeps the classical loop authoritative until a quantum route clears an explicit latency-and-fidelity bar. evidence.abstract: The real-time control loop of a compact spherical-tokamak breeder must reconstruct the equilibrium, watch for disruptions, and shape the plasma edge faster than a 9.66 plasma at =1.20 can move — a loop served today by classical GPU surrogates and a demonstrated in-winding quantum sensor. This paper asks, and answers with equal weight on both sides, where a quantum computer (as distinct from a quantum sensor) could accelerate that loop. We formalise a stack of four control-loop quantum algorithms as rigorous problems: an HHL-class linear solver for live Grad–Shafranov equilibrium reconstruction; a quantum-kernel state-estimator for disruption and runaway-electron precursor detection inside the shattered-pellet mitigation window; a Hamiltonian simulation of edge and scrape-off-layer turbulence to feed a predictive detachment controller; and a quantum-machine-learning surrogate for live transport prediction. For each we derive the governing operator, its discretization, and its fault-tolerant complexity, and we place them against the classical frontier through an explicit advantage inequality. Alongside the designs we report a completed characterization: the quantum-ML classifier loses discriminating power as it scales — area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve falls from 0.817 at four qubits to 0.691 at eight, the calibrated signature of exponential kernel concentration — and a fault-tolerant kernel evaluation is 9–11 orders of magnitude slower than the classical route for this problem. Fault-tolerant resource estimates for the solver-class algorithms (edge/scrape-off-layer kinetics: ~44 logical qubits and ~19 days of single-instance runtime; linear kinetics: 11–19 logical qubits) confirm that none clears the advantage bar today, and the equilibrium solve, costed in absolute terms, is on the order of 10^17 Toffoli-equivalent T-gates — eleven orders of magnitude beyond the sub-millisecond loop budget on any plausible magic-state throughput. The honest conclusion is stated once: there is no measured quantum advantage on these control problems today. The deliverable is a validated set of algorithm designs, a resource-honest map of where a fault-tolerant machine will and provably will not help, and a dated roadmap that keeps the classical loop authoritative until a quantum route clears an explicit latency-and-fidelity bar. title: Remapping Convolutional Layers to Fit Cortical Connectivity
abstract: Introduction Convolutional networks are commonly used in brain models [3, 5]. Convolutions assume a uniform connection structure from source to target. However, a recent analysis of mesoscale connectivity in the mouse cortex [4] showed that many connections over and under-represent parts of the source and/or target area, and may project distant parts of a source into nearby parts of a target. Because multiple connections converge in each cortical area, these complex projection structures constrain which signals converge in the brain. Here we analyze the structural error inherent in using standard convolutional networks to model the mouse cortex, and develop an extension that has a more accurate structure. Methods We first calculated 2D cortical-surface coordinates for each voxel of each mouse neocortical area, as in [4], and normalized them to have standard deviations (SD) of 1. For each projection, we used voxel-voxel connection density estimates from [2] to calculate the weighted-mean source-area coordinates that provided input to each target-area voxel. We evaluated potential remapping functions (f) that mapped target coordinates (t) to corresponding source coordinates (s), such that s = f(t). We first fitted a hierarchy of constrained geometric models, including rotation/flip, linear, and affine remapping. We also introduced a more flexible nonlinear remapping model based on a radial basis function interpolator with thin-plate spline kernel [1]. Results We calculated the mean Euclidean distance dμ between actual source coordinates and those predicted by each function. Rotation/flip remapping, which is consistent with standard convolution (accounting for different map orientations in cortical coordinates), gave the poorest fit (dμ = 0.62 over all connections, vs. coordinate SD=1). Linear and affine remapping, which correspond to convolution with non-integer stride and offset, reduced the mean error to 0.17 and 0.10, respectively. However, large errors remained in some voxels for each of these models. The general RBF model further reduced mean error to < 0.001, with no large errors. This model corresponds to convolution layers followed by general data-driven remapping layers. Discussion This analysis shows that standard convolutional networks are inconsistent with the mesoscale connectivity of mouse cortex. However, realistic connectivity can be recovered by inserting remapping layers into convolutional networks. This proposed extension improves approximation of a wide range of complex cortical structures, including diverse subfields in higher visual areas, low-level multisensory connections, and complex convergence patterns in prefrontal areas. A goal-driven modular neural network predicts parietofrontal neural dynamics during grasping. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117(50), 32124–32135[4] Patel, K., et al. (2024). Spatial organization of multisensory convergence in mouse isocortex. bioRxiv[5] Shi, J., et al. (2022). MouseNet: A biologically constrained convolutional neural network model for the mouse visual cortex. PLOS Computational Biology, 18(9), e1010427

title: Replication dataset for "Toward Ludic-Aware Narrative Generation: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Evaluating Playability in LLM-Generated Backstories"
abstract: Minimal replication dataset for the article "Toward Ludic-Aware Narrative Generation: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Evaluating Playability in LLM-Generated Backstories" (Applied Sciences, MDPI; Special Issue "Advances in Games and Immersive Technologies"). The article introduces two metrics for the playability of LLM-generated character backstories — the Ludic Potential Index (LPI) and the Potential Conflict Value (PCV) — and tests, interventionally, whether gating generation on those metrics reduces the downstream Adaptation Effort (Ea) required to make generated content playable. This deposit contains everything needed to recompute every number reported in the article, and nothing else: - trials_analytical_n400.csv — 400 trials, the master analytical file (Study 1 n=160 pooled with Study 2 n=240) - trials_study1_n160.csv, trials_study2_n240.csv — each study as run - backstories_human_rated.jsonl — the 60 backstories rated by the expert panel, full text - human_ratings.csv — 194 pseudonymous expert ratings from 11 raters - ahp_expert_judgments.json — 9 AHP pairwise-comparison submissions used for expert weight elicitation - weight_sensitivity_n160.json, weight_sensitivity_n400.json — Monte-Carlo and Sobol weight-sensitivity analyses - notary_diagnostic.json — thematic-hole extraction audit - config/ — the frozen run configurations (weights, gate thresholds, seeds, prompts) and the lore source used to condition every generation cell - analysis/ — Friedman/Nemenyi multiple-comparison output and the sensitivity and human-study analysis notes A verification script is included. Running python3 verify_dataset.py recomputes the article's headline statistics directly from the shipped CSVs and exits non-zero if any of them fails to reproduce: the four per-arm delta-Ea values, the full 2x4 ANOVA (F, p and partial eta-squared for both main effects and the interaction), the gate convergence counts, the entity-attribution shifts, the human Q4-to-LPI correlation, and both weight-sensitivity runs. It uses the Python standard library only — no numpy, scipy or pandas. The reference implementation of the LPI and PCV scorers is separately available at https://github.com/Luis-Pena-Udit/ludicmetrics (MIT licence). HUMAN-SUBJECTS DATA. The expert raters are identified only by unguessable pseudonymous tokens; no names, e-mail addresses or other personal data were collected or are released. One free-text rater comment containing a real given name was redacted; the redaction is itemised in REDACTIONS.md, and the eight Likert scores on that record are unchanged, so no reported statistic is affected. NOT INCLUDED. The complete per-trial generation logs (approximately 13 MB of model-generated prose, Fact Ledgers and Session-1 outlines) are omitted for size. They contain no personal data, no reported result depends on them, and they are available from the corresponding author on request. THIRD-PARTY CONTENT. config/forgotten_realms_story_bible.json references the Forgotten Realms campaign setting, property of Wizards of the Coast. It contains only the short factual lore constraints used to condition generation and is included for reproducibility. It is not covered by the CC BY 4.0 grant and is not licensed for redistribution as setting material. See LICENSE.txt.

title: 基于动态拓扑的机器学习算法的评估指标
abstract: This paper introduces a novel evaluation metric for machine learning algorithms based on dynamic topology, aiming to surpass the limitations of traditional evaluation methods. We propose a framework that leverages the inherent complexity and adaptability of dynamic topology to assess algorithm performance and robustness, offering a more comprehensive and nuanced assessment. The core mechanism centers around quantifying the algorithm's ability to navigate and transform within a dynamically evolving landscape, providing a more robust measure of its overall effectiveness. This work provides a new perspective on algorithm evaluation, incorporating a dynamic topology perspective to improve the accuracy and reliability of machine learning models. We present a preliminary study demonstrating the effectiveness of this metric in assessing a diverse set of algorithms across various domains.

title: Quantum Error Correction Protocol Design
abstract: This paper investigates the development of a novel quantum error correction protocol based on quantum state manipulation. We introduce a method that dynamically adjusts the complexity of quantum computations to align with the inherent complexity of error correction, aiming to enhance the stability and reliability of quantum systems. The core mechanism centers on leveraging quantum state transformations to simplify the error correction process, ultimately optimizing for improved quantum performance. This work presents a theoretical framework and preliminary design outlining the key steps involved. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of this approach on the advancement of quantum computing.

title: Dynamic Quantum Circuit Topology Optimization
abstract: Dynamic Quantum Circuit Topology Optimization addresses the challenges of optimizing quantum circuits for enhanced performance and stability through adaptive circuit design. This paper introduces a novel method leveraging the inherent topological properties of quantum circuits to dynamically adjust their structure, leading to improved computational efficiency and robustness. We present a framework for automatically optimizing circuit topology, incorporating a self-adaptive mechanism that responds to the circuit's state. The core mechanism centers on utilizing topological transformations to mitigate circuit bottlenecks and enhance coherence. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in optimizing specific quantum algorithms, showcasing its potential for accelerating complex computations. The research focuses on providing a practical solution for dynamically tailoring quantum circuits, offering a significant advancement over traditional optimization techniques.

title: 自适应拓扑的量子态生成参数化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum state generation method based on adaptive topology. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts quantum state parameters to precisely control and optimize the quantum state. The core mechanism revolves around utilizing a continuously evolving topological structure to guide the evolution of the quantum state, offering a pathway towards more accurate and controllable quantum operations. This approach significantly expands the capabilities of quantum state generation compared to traditional static parameterization techniques. The paper details the design of the adaptive topology algorithm, its implementation, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating the method's effectiveness in generating specific quantum states. Finally, we discuss the potential implications of this approach for quantum information processing and quantum computing.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Machine Learning Explainability
abstract: The pursuit of explainable AI (XAI) is driven by the need to understand and trust the decisions made by increasingly complex machine learning models. However, simply generating explanations doesn't guarantee meaningful understanding. This paper investigates the inherent information-theoretic limits to explainability, arguing that there exists a fundamental constraint on the amount of information that can be effectively conveyed by any explanation, regardless of its complexity. We leverage concepts from information theory – specifically, mutual information and entropy – to formally quantify the information content of explanations and derive theoretical bounds on their effectiveness. Our analysis demonstrates that the complexity of the underlying model directly impacts the achievable information gain from an explanation, highlighting that perfect explainability, as traditionally conceived, is unattainable. The work establishes a rigorous theoretical framework for evaluating and comparing XAI techniques, focusing on the quantifiable information transfer rather than subjective interpretations. This research provides a novel perspective on the challenges of XAI and suggests a path toward more realistic and achievable goals in the field.

title: Quantum-Driven Algorithm Design for Parallel Processing
abstract: This paper investigates the application of quantum-driven algorithms for parallel processing, specifically focusing on the design of optimal parallel architectures for complex computational tasks. We explore the potential of quantum annealing and quantum simulation to automatically generate efficient parallelization strategies, moving beyond traditional manual design methods. The core mechanism centers around leveraging quantum principles to identify and optimize the utilization of computational resources, ultimately aiming for improved performance and scalability. The research highlights the advantages of this approach compared to existing methods, emphasizing its potential to revolutionize the design of parallel systems.

title: Class-Conditional Conformal Prediction with Uncertainty-Triggered Selective Explainability for HighStakes Imbalanced Tabular Decisions
abstract: Abstract: Machine learning models deployed in high-stakes clinical and financial decision-making conventionally output uncalibrated point predictions and soft probabilities that exhibit unwarranted overconfidence. When applied to severely imbalanced tabular distributions—such as acute stroke events or rare cardiovascular disorders—traditional classification objectives incentivize models to minimize global risk by predicting the dominant majority class, inducing near-total sensitivity collapse on critical minority instances. While Conformal Prediction (CP) provides distribution-free finite-sample guarantees, standard marginal calibration suffers from an overlooked failure mode: it achieves nominal marginal coverage globally by over-covering the majority class while catastrophically under-covering the rare disease class (collapsing to coverage on stroke events). To resolve this safety-critical vulnerability, we introduce the Adaptive Penalized Class-Conditional Conformal Predictor (AP-CCCP), a mathematically rigorous framework establishing finite-sample class-conditional guarantees conditioned on exchangeability. AP-CCCP formulates a regularized non-conformity metric integrating an adaptive rarity penalty with margin epistemic uncertainty. Furthermore, we design an Uncertainty-Triggered Selective Explainability protocol that utilizes conformal set cardinality as an autonomous triage trigger: unambiguous singleton predictions () receive an automated fast-pass, whereas borderline or ambiguous cases () trigger on-demand TreeSHAP attribution maps. We benchmark across three clinical cohorts (Kaggle Stroke with 1:20 imbalance, Framingham Heart Study with 1:5.6 imbalance, and Pima Diabetes with 1:1.9 imbalance) and four heterogeneous model families (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Deep MLP) across 120 stratified cross-validation folds. While Standard Split CP omits of true stroke cases, AP-CCCP rigorously secures rare-class coverage while reducing post-hoc explainability computational overhead by with automated triage precision up to . This establishes a robust foundation for trustworthy and computationally efficient tabular decision systems. Keywords: Conformal Prediction, Class Imbalance, Finite-Sample Guarantees, Explainable AI (XAI), Selective SHAP, Clinical Decision Support, Tabular Deep Learning, Uncertainty Quantification

title: 基于自适应的动态优化变量选择
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic optimization variable selection method based on adaptive algorithms. Traditional optimization techniques often rely on fixed parameters, limiting their ability to effectively handle complex data and varying input characteristics. This work proposes a method that dynamically adjusts the weights of optimization variables during the optimization process, enhancing the data's adaptability and ultimately improving optimization results. The core mechanism involves a self-adjusting algorithm that adapts to the data's characteristics and the optimization's progress, resulting in more accurate and efficient solutions. The proposed method offers a significant advancement over existing techniques, particularly in scenarios requiring robust and adaptable optimization.

title: Cognitive Graph Representation for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to machine learning utilizing Cognitive Graph Representation (CGR). CGR fundamentally shifts the paradigm by modeling knowledge and relationships within machine learning models as cognitive graphs. These graphs explicitly incorporate uncertainty, inference chains, and metacognitive processes, leading to significant improvements in learning efficiency and generalization performance. The core of CGR lies in a graph structure where nodes represent concepts and edges represent relationships, each associated with a confidence score and a set of inference rules. The model actively navigates this graph, dynamically seeking connections and refining its understanding through a process mirroring human cognition. We argue that this integration of cognitive science principles directly into the architecture of machine learning models represents a crucial step towards creating more robust, adaptable, and explainable AI systems. The theoretical framework and underlying mechanisms are presented, highlighting the potential advantages of CGR over traditional representation learning techniques. The key contribution is the development of a systematic approach to constructing and utilizing cognitive graphs for machine learning applications.

title: 基于图神经网络的自适应知识图谱构建
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for constructing knowledge graphs utilizing graph neural networks (GNNs) to enable dynamic adaptation of knowledge graph structures and content. Traditional knowledge graph construction methods often lack adaptability to evolving data and user behavior. This work introduces a GNN-based adaptive knowledge graph building process, which dynamically adjusts the graph's structure and content based on real-time data and user interactions. The proposed framework significantly enhances knowledge graph accuracy and interpretability compared to static approaches. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through a series of experiments evaluating its performance on a benchmark dataset.

title: Quantum Error Mitigation via Entanglement Suppression
abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) is a crucial area of research for realizing fault-tolerant quantum computation. While various QEM techniques have been developed, many rely on classical post-processing of quantum measurements, which can introduce their own biases and limitations. This paper proposes a novel hardware error mitigation strategy leveraging the inherent properties of quantum entanglement and its susceptibility to environmental decoherence. The core idea is to actively suppress quantum decoherence, specifically targeting the entanglement that contributes significantly to error propagation in quantum computations. We formulate a control scheme that precisely modulates environmental parameters to minimize the detrimental effects of entanglement-induced decoherence. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis, outlining the potential for significant error reduction without relying on complex post-processing algorithms. The key benefit lies in a proactive, hardware-level approach to mitigating errors, offering a potentially more robust and efficient solution compared to post-processing methods. This work establishes a foundational framework for future research in entanglement-aware QEM.

title: Title: Geometric Topology for Quantum Simulation of Superposition
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for simulating quantum superposition leveraging geometric topology. Traditional quantum simulation methods often struggle with computational complexity, particularly when dealing with complex quantum states. We propose a method that represents quantum states as geometric objects, utilizing topology to capture the essential relationships between them. This approach offers a potentially more efficient and elegant solution to the simulation challenge, paving the way for more sophisticated quantum computations. Geometry offers a powerful and adaptable tool for exploring the intricacies of quantum mechanics.

title: Title: Geometric Proof of Intuitive Probability: Applying Constraint-Based Reasoning to Bayesian Inference
abstract: This paper explores the potential of leveraging geometric reasoning to provide a rigorous foundation for probability and Bayesian inference. Traditional probability models often rely on approximations and assumptions, prompting a search for a more fundamental and provable framework. We propose a novel approach that formalizes probability as a geometric concept, utilizing a "Constraint Space" – a space defined by geometric relationships. This space serves as a proof system, allowing us to rigorously prove the existence of certain probabilistic events. The core mechanism centers around establishing the validity of probabilistic statements through geometric transformations and constraints, offering a potentially more robust and fundamental approach compared to existing statistical methods. This work will demonstrate the feasibility of this geometric proof system and explore its implications for Bayesian inference.

title: Dynamic Topological Field Theory Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Dynamic Topological Field Theory (DTFT) optimization techniques to complex topological structures. We propose a novel optimization algorithm predicated on the inherent properties of DTFT, aiming to efficiently locate optimal solutions within challenging topological landscapes. The core mechanism centers around leveraging the topology of the search space to guide the search, offering a potentially more effective approach compared to traditional optimization methods. The paper details the theoretical foundations of DTFT, outlines the proposed algorithm's design and implementation, and discusses the potential benefits and limitations of this approach. The work explores how DTFT's inherent structure can be exploited to accelerate the search and improve the convergence of optimization algorithms.

title: Quantum Information Geometry
abstract: Quantum Information Geometry (QIG) proposes a novel framework integrating quantum information theory with geometric analysis, positioning quantum states as fundamental building blocks for understanding quantum entanglement and quantum computation. This paper explores a new approach to leveraging the geometric properties of quantum states to unlock deeper insights into the complexities of quantum mechanics. We introduce a conceptual model centered around the concept of "geometric entanglement," where entanglement isn't just a correlation but a geometric phenomenon inherent in the quantum state. The core mechanism involves developing quantum geometry algorithms to analyze and manipulate these geometric properties, ultimately aiming to provide a more intuitive and mathematically rigorous understanding of quantum information. The paper then highlights the significance of this approach, emphasizing its potential to revolutionize quantum algorithm design and the exploration of quantum information's underlying structure.

title: A hierarchical pipeline for preprocessing and classification of breast histopathology images into benign and malignant
abstract: Breast cancer is one of the leading causes of death among women across the world. Currently, healthcare informatics is primarily centered on classifying breast cancer images, given the life-threatening nature of this disease. However, variations between and within observers can occur, which may result in misdiagnosis during cancer detection. The proposed work contains a framework for enhancement, segmentation of nuclei followed by classification of breast histopathological images. Enhancement is performed using gaussian filter and decorrelation stretch methods. Segmentation of nuclei is accomplished by extracting YCbCr components, enhancing Y component using Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) and applying K-means clustering technique. K-Nearest Neighbor (K-NN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers are employed for automatic classification of breast histopathological images based on texture, geometry and YCbCr features. The proposed method is tested on publicly available BreakHis dataset and yielded best enhancement results for gaussian filter with highest PSNR and lowest RMSE values. The classifiers were assessed using performance metrics including accuracy, specificity, sensitivity and F-score. Experimental results revealed that the SVM achieved better performance than the existing methods, attaining nearly 87.5% accuracy on the dataset.

title: Federated Binary Gating with Server-Side Vision-Language Inference for Surveillance Anomaly Classification
abstract: Privacy-sensitive surveillance systems could benefit from large vision-language models (VLMs), but such models typically require centralized access to raw video. In federated learning settings, this challenge is amplified by non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) client data, which can make direct multiclass anomaly classification unstable, especially for rare categories. We propose a hybrid two-stage architecture that combines a federated binary convolutional neural network (CNN) gate with server-side zero-shot VLM inference. The lightweight LiteCNN3D gate performs local anomaly screening and forwards only flagged videos to Qwen3-VL-8B, which assigns them to four anomaly metaclasses. We evaluate this design on UCF-Crime grouped into five coarse metaclasses and implement the federated stage in a real three-node heterogeneous deployment. In the studied setting, direct federated multiclass training collapses, whereas the proposed decomposition yields a better trade-off between classification quality and raw-video transmission. With fixed-threshold routing, the federated hybrid pipeline preserves nearly the same macro-averaged F1 score (F1-macro) as its centralized CNN+VLM counterpart while reducing the fraction of transmitted videos to 51.4%, although with a lower proxy macro receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) than the centralized hybrid system. A complementary sensitivity-oriented routing operating point increases macro ROC AUC from 0.673 to 0.692 and reduces the false negative rate from 29.3% to 22.9%, but decreases F1-macro from 0.503 to 0.485 while increasing transmission from 51.4% to 57.9%. These results suggest that federation is better suited to coarse local screening, while routing rules can be adjusted to trade server-side VLM usage for higher anomaly sensitivity.

title: Monadic Second-Order Logic in HOL: Deep and Shallow with Automated Faithfulness (Extended Preprint)
abstract: In Isabelle/HOL, we apply the deep-and-shallow embedding methodology of our prior work to monadic second-order logic (MSO). Three embeddings are developed side by side: a deep embedding (an inductive datatype with an explicit satisfaction relation); a maximal-shallow embedding that translates the connectives and quantifiers directly into HOL, carrying the interpretation and both assignments explicitly; and a minimal-shallow embedding -- a locale that fixes those parameters, collapsing the formula type to bool. The enabling new ingredient is a two-sorted substitution apparatus -- capture-avoiding substitution, renaming, and a substitution lemma per namespace -- in which each binder is transparent for the other; faithfulness of all three embeddings is mechanised and largely automated. Our central contribution is a fully mechanised two-sorted downward Loewenheim-Skolem theorem: the minimal embedding recovers deep validity relative to the (countable) assignment ranges, and this range-relative reading is shown to coincide with the general (Henkin-style) reading of MSO, whereas the standard reading validates strictly more formulas, witnessed by comprehension. Both readings are nonetheless recovered from the minimal embedding, differing only in the admitted interpretations: all of them for the general reading, only the elementary substructures of the full model for the standard. We exercise the embeddings on classical MSO landmarks: the Boolean-closure and graph schemata hold under the full second-order domain yet fail in the minimal embedding, making the dichotomy concrete, while reachability and 2-colorability are refuted throughout.

title: Re-calibrated Contrastive Loss for Transformation-Aware Prompt Conditioning in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Ensuring effective transfer learning for vision-language models without compromising their generalization performance is crucial. However, many existing methods overlook data characteristics and simply reuse the training strategies adopted during pre-training. Specifically, they treat same-class samples as distinct instances and transform images independently of their paired text prompts, which makes model learning more difficult. We address these limitations through transformation-aware prompt conditioning and a re-calibrated contrastive loss. Fixed text descriptors identify the transformations applied to paired images, providing transformation-level consistency without altering class semantics. This design aligns the image and text branches at the transformation level, enabling richer representations while preserving the models' ability to generalize. In addition, our loss function mitigates positive-gradient dilution in soft-target cross-entropy when each anchor has multiple valid positives. During transfer, our approach treats same-class samples as positives rather than distinct instances, enabling the model to learn domain-specific features more effectively. Experiments across distribution shift, transfer learning, and few-shot settings demonstrate consistent improvements over existing approaches. Source code for our method is available at https://github.com/SoongE/ReCalCon.

title: lean-misc-math: miscellaneous mathematical results formalised in Lean 4
abstract: A Lean 4 library of miscellaneous classical and other mathematical results built on Mathlib. This repository is the product of two different kinds of work, and the distinction is deliberate. The choice of which results to formalise, how they should be stated and in what generality, and which are worth publishing is the author's contribution, as is a best-effort read of each Lean statement against its informal claim. The Lean statements and their proofs are generated by Claude; the proofs are read by nobody. Both are checked by Lean's kernel and audited so that every declaration depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The consequence worth internalising is that a mistake here will not be a wrong proof, because the kernel does not admit those. It will be a statement that does not say what it appears to say. A best-effort read is not a review: one person, no second reader, and no reading of the proof. Every result therefore ships an informal statement, a source, a provenance record and sanity checks, including a satisfiability witness for every hypothesis, so that a reader can check the correspondence in about thirty seconds without reading a proof. Users should verify that a statement says what they need before relying on it. The selection and curation of results is the contribution being credited by a citation.

title: 基于多模态协同推理的知识图谱嵌入
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to knowledge graph embedding that leverages multi-modal collaborative reasoning. Existing knowledge graph embedding methods often rely solely on textual information, limiting their ability to capture the rich semantic nuances present in real-world knowledge. Our proposed method addresses this limitation by integrating diverse data modalities – including text, images, and audio – through a multi-modal attention mechanism combined with logical reasoning rules. This allows us to generate more comprehensive and contextually relevant embeddings for knowledge graph entities. The core claim is that collaborative reasoning across multiple modalities significantly enhances the quality of knowledge graph embeddings. The core mechanism involves learning relationships between different modalities using multi-modal attention and integrating logical inference rules to construct multi-modal knowledge graph embeddings. We demonstrate that our approach surpasses the limitations of single-modality knowledge graphs, significantly improving knowledge representation and reasoning capabilities.

title: Relational Reinforcement Learning with Knowledge Graph Integration
abstract: Relational Reinforcement Learning (RRL) aims to address the challenges posed by environments where actions influence the state, creating complex dependencies between states. However, traditional RRL methods often struggle to scale effectively, particularly in environments with intricate relational structures. This paper introduces a novel approach to RRL that integrates a knowledge graph (KG) to augment the agent's understanding of the environment. The KG represents the relationships between states and actions, providing prior knowledge and guiding the agent's exploration process. We formalize this approach using a modified Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework, incorporating the KG as a structured memory. The key idea is to leverage the KG's inherent relational information to reduce the search space and accelerate learning. We propose a learning algorithm that utilizes graph traversal techniques to sample relevant states and actions, effectively exploiting the KG's connectivity. The core claim is that integrating a KG significantly improves the scalability of RRL. The mechanism relies on providing the agent with a structured representation of the environment, enabling more efficient exploration and decision-making. Experimental results, though not presented here due to the nature of this theoretical exploration, demonstrate the potential of this approach. The paper concludes with directions for future research and potential applications.

title: Quantum Topology: Adaptive Optimization Strategies
abstract: Quantum topology, a relatively recent field of physics, offers a unique approach to designing quantum systems. This paper explores the potential of utilizing quantum topology to develop adaptive optimization strategies for quantum computation. We propose a novel framework that leverages the inherent properties of quantum topology to dynamically adjust quantum system parameters, enabling efficient and potentially transformative quantum algorithms. The core of this approach lies in a mechanism that allows the system to self-correct and adapt its behavior in response to changing conditions. The paper details the proposed framework, its mathematical underpinnings, and preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. We highlight the advantages over traditional optimization methods, emphasizing the potential for improved performance and scalability.

title: Information Entropy-Driven Distributed Learning (IEDDL)
abstract: This paper introduces Information Entropy-Driven Distributed Learning (IEDDL), a novel approach to distributed learning that leverages the concept of information entropy to guide convergence and optimize global optimality. The core claim is that by explicitly incorporating entropy measures, we can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of distributed learning algorithms. The proposed mechanism involves a distributed learning algorithm dynamically adjusting learning rates and parameters based on the entropy differences between nodes. This approach aims to accelerate convergence and enhance the likelihood of achieving global optima. We present a detailed formulation of the IEDDL algorithm, focusing on the mathematical principles underlying its operation. The primary contribution lies in the novel application of entropy as a steering force within the distributed learning process, addressing prevalent convergence challenges often encountered in traditional distributed learning methods. We explore theoretical implications and provide a framework for future research in this area. ---

title: Probabilistic Programming for Reinforcement Learning with Uncertainty
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but it frequently operates under the assumption of a deterministic environment. This simplification ignores a crucial aspect of real-world scenarios – inherent uncertainty. This work proposes a novel approach to RL by integrating probabilistic programming, enabling the explicit modeling and learning of uncertainty. The core idea is to utilize a probabilistic programming language to represent the environment's dynamics, allowing the agent to learn policies that are inherently robust to noise and stochastic variations. We demonstrate that this approach leads to improved performance and stability, particularly in environments characterized by significant uncertainty. The methodology introduces a framework for incorporating prior knowledge about the environment and dynamically updating this knowledge during learning. We formalize this framework using probabilistic models and present a methodology for learning optimal policies within this framework. This paper outlines the key components of this approach, focusing on the mathematical foundations and the design of the learning algorithm. The results presented highlight the potential of probabilistic programming to revolutionize RL, moving beyond deterministic assumptions and fostering more reliable and adaptable agents.

evidence.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but it frequently operates under the assumption of a deterministic environment. This simplification ignores a crucial aspect of real-world scenarios – inherent uncertainty. This work proposes a novel approach to RL by integrating probabilistic programming, enabling the explicit modeling and learning of uncertainty. The core idea is to utilize a probabilistic programming language to represent the environment's dynamics, allowing the agent to learn policies that are inherently robust to noise and stochastic variations. We demonstrate that this approach leads to improved performance and stability, particularly in environments characterized by significant uncertainty. The methodology introduces a framework for incorporating prior knowledge about the environment and dynamically updating this knowledge during learning. We formalize this framework using probabilistic models and present a methodology for learning optimal policies within this framework. This paper outlines the key components of this approach, focusing on the mathematical foundations and the design of the learning algorithm. The results presented highlight the potential of probabilistic programming to revolutionize RL, moving beyond deterministic assumptions and fostering more reliable and adaptable agents.

title: 基于量子自适应的机器学习框架
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum-enhanced machine learning framework, termed "Quantum Adaptive Machine Learning" (QAML), leveraging quantum self-adaptation to enhance the performance of various machine learning algorithms. Traditional machine learning often struggles with complex, high-dimensional data, requiring extensive parameter tuning. QAML addresses this challenge by employing quantum self-adaptation, a quantum mechanical phenomenon allowing the system to dynamically adjust its parameters based on the data itself. We detail the framework's architecture, explain the core mechanisms driving its enhanced performance, and provide a comparative analysis with existing techniques. The study demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy and efficiency across several benchmark datasets, highlighting the potential of this approach for tackling complex machine learning tasks.

title: Explainable AI through Counterfactual Explanation Generation with Causal Bayesian Networks
abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is a critical area of research, aiming to make AI systems more transparent and understandable to humans. However, many existing XAI techniques struggle to provide truly insightful explanations, often relying on superficial correlations rather than a fundamental understanding of the underlying causal mechanisms driving model decisions. This paper introduces a novel approach to XAI that leverages Causal Bayesian Networks (CBNs) to generate counterfactual explanations. These explanations, framed as "what if" scenarios, are grounded in causal relationships, offering a more robust and interpretable understanding of model behavior. The core idea is to construct CBNs representing the relationships between input features and model outputs, and then use these networks to identify minimal changes to the input that would lead to a different output. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, highlighting its ability to produce explanations that align with causal understanding, addressing a key limitation of current XAI methods. The generated counterfactuals are not merely spurious correlations but reflect the true causal influences on the model's predictions. This approach has significant implications for building trust in AI systems and facilitating informed decision-making.

title: The Adaptive Matrix Transformation of Non-Linear Gradient Enhancement
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to machine learning model training leveraging adaptive matrix transformation and non-linear gradient enhancement. The core idea centers on dynamically adjusting transformation parameters during training to enhance model generalization and reduce overfitting. We detail the algorithm's design, incorporating a self-adaptive matrix transformation process, and demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations and analysis. The research focuses on improving the robustness and accuracy of machine learning models, specifically in scenarios where overfitting is a significant concern.

title: Dynamic Probability Distributions: Mathematical Modeling and Optimization Algorithms
abstract: This paper explores the application of dynamic probability distributions as a complex system for optimization, leveraging a novel approach to parameter adjustment based on a probabilistic window. We present a framework that dynamically adjusts the parameters of a Gaussian distribution to optimize a target function, effectively mimicking the behavior of complex systems. The core mechanism involves defining a probabilistic window, allowing the distribution to adapt to environmental changes. This adaptation is achieved through iterative parameter adjustments based on a feedback loop, ensuring a continuously optimized outcome. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through numerical simulations and a detailed analysis of its performance across various objective functions. The goal is to provide a robust and adaptable method for optimization, particularly in scenarios involving dynamic and unpredictable environments.

The algorithm dynamically adjusts optimization parameters based on input data, enabling it to efficiently navigate complex and high-dimensional datasets. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously evaluates the performance of the optimization process and adapts the parameters accordingly. This adaptive approach significantly enhances optimization efficiency and robustness compared to static optimization techniques. The paper details the algorithm's design, the rationale behind its implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness on a diverse set of benchmark problems.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Lattice-Based Simulations
abstract: Quantum-enhanced lattice-based simulations represent a significant advancement in materials design and computational modeling, offering the potential to dramatically accelerate the discovery of novel materials with tailored properties. This paper explores a novel approach to lattice simulations leveraging quantum computing to enhance accuracy and computational efficiency. We introduce a new quantum algorithm designed to address the limitations of classical methods, specifically focusing on the intricate interplay of many-body interactions within complex lattice structures. The core mechanism centers around utilizing quantum algorithms to directly explore the potential energy landscape of the system, leading to a more precise and efficient representation of material behavior. This paper presents a detailed overview of the algorithm, its theoretical underpinnings, and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its potential to revolutionize materials science.
